stem: A job must fire only on merged pull requests, not on PRs closed without merging. Which trigger and condition pair is correct?

options.text: on: pull_request types: [closed] with if: github.event.pull_request.merged == true
on: pull_request_target types: [closed] with if: github.event.action == 'merged'
on: push to the base branch with if: github.event.pull_request.merged == true
on: pull_request types: [closed] with if: github.event.action == 'merged'

explanationCorrect: The pull_request event has no merged activity type. You listen for the closed activity and check the boolean github.event.pull_request.merged to distinguish a real merge from an abandoned close.
explanationIncorrect: pull_request_target fires in the base repo's context for fork safety, but the activity type 'merged' does not exist — you still need types: [closed] plus the merged boolean check. A push to the base branch fires on every push, not only merges, and carries no pull_request payload so github.event.pull_request.merged is undefined. Checking github.event.action == 'merged' on pull_request fails because the action value is 'closed', never 'merged' — the merged boolean is a separate field on the pull_request object.

stem: New pushes to a PR branch should cancel that branch's in-progress workflow, but runs on main must never be cancelled. Which configuration achieves this?

options.text: concurrency group on github.workflow with cancel-in-progress: true globally
concurrency on ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}, cancel-in-progress excludes main via expression
strategy.max-parallel: 1 on each job to serialize all branch runs
concurrency group on github.ref with cancel-in-progress: ${{ always() }}

explanationCorrect: A concurrency group that includes github.ref serializes runs per branch, and expressing cancel-in-progress as a conditional expression lets main opt out while feature branches cancel their own older runs.
explanationIncorrect: cancel-in-progress: true with no expression cancels in-progress runs for every group, including main, violating the requirement. max-parallel limits how many legs of a matrix run concurrently within a single workflow run — it does nothing across separate runs triggered by successive commits. Using always() as the cancel-in-progress expression evaluates to true in all cases, so it would cancel main runs too. The correct approach is a per-ref group with cancel-in-progress evaluated as an expression excluding refs/heads/main.

stem: A composite action computes a value in one step and a later step needs to read it. Which mechanism correctly passes the value between steps?

options.text: Write name=value to $GITHUB_OUTPUT in a step with an id, then read steps.<id>.outputs.<name>
Use save-state in the first step to expose the value to later steps
Set a shell variable with export NAME=value so it persists across steps
Read steps.<id>.result in the later step without writing to any file

explanationCorrect: Appending name=value to $GITHUB_OUTPUT publishes a named step output, and a later step reads it as steps.<id>.outputs.<name> because the first step carries an id.
explanationIncorrect: save-state passes data from a JavaScript action's main phase to its own post phase, not between composite action steps. Each step runs in its own shell process, so export sets the variable only within that step's shell and it does not survive into the next step. There is no generic steps.<id>.result field for arbitrary values; result exists only for a job's outcome status, not for data a step produced.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: A workflow must authenticate to AWS for deployment without any long-lived keys stored as secrets. The team has configured an IAM OIDC identity provider that trusts GitHub. Which combination of workflow settings completes the setup?

options.text: Grant permissions: id-token: read and use the aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials action with role-to-assume
Grant permissions: id-token: write and use aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials with role-to-assume
Store AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY as org secrets and reference them with aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials
Grant permissions: contents: write and pass secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN to the AWS SDK via the environment

explanationCorrect: The workflow needs permissions: id-token: write (not read) to request the OIDC token from GitHub's provider. The aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials action then exchanges that token for temporary AWS credentials by assuming the IAM role.
explanationIncorrect: id-token: read is insufficient; the job must be able to create (write) the token, not merely read it, so the run would fail with a permission error. Storing long-lived access keys as org secrets is exactly the standing-credential pattern OIDC replaces, and the action would use the static keys rather than federated credentials. The GITHUB_TOKEN authenticates only to GitHub's own APIs, not AWS, so passing it to the AWS SDK accomplishes nothing.

stem: A workflow must call a reusable workflow in another repository and pass a secret to it. Which syntax is valid for the calling job?

options.text: Add uses: owner/repo/.github/workflows/file.yml@ref as a step and pass the secret with with:
Set jobs.<id>.uses: owner/repo/.github/workflows/file.yml@ref with a secrets: block
Use run: gh workflow run file.yml and export the secret as an environment variable
Set jobs.<id>.uses: for the workflow and pass the secret under the with: key

explanationCorrect: A reusable workflow is invoked at the job level with uses:, and secrets are passed through the secrets: keyword (or secrets: inherit), not through with: which is for non-sensitive inputs.
explanationIncorrect: Reusable workflows cannot be called as a step; they must be referenced at the job level with jobs.<id>.uses, so putting uses under steps is wrong. gh workflow run triggers a separate workflow_dispatch run rather than composing it into this run, and it cannot return outputs back to the caller. The with: key passes inputs, not secrets; secrets must use the dedicated secrets: block to keep them masked and secure.

stem: Tests must run against Node 18, 20, and 22 on both ubuntu-latest and windows-latest, covering all six combinations from a single job definition. Which feature handles this?

options.text: The fromJSON function applied directly to runs-on without a strategy block
A reusable workflow called once per combination via workflow_call
A build matrix under strategy.matrix with node-version and os axes
A shell for-loop inside one run step iterating over all six pairs

explanationCorrect: A matrix defines the axes (node-version and os) and GitHub expands them into one job per combination automatically, so three versions across two operating systems produce all six runs from a single job definition.
explanationIncorrect: fromJSON can build a matrix value from a computed JSON string, but on its own applied to runs-on without strategy.matrix it does not expand combinations into separate jobs. Calling a reusable workflow once per combination requires six separate caller jobs, defeating the single-definition requirement. A shell for-loop runs everything inside one job on one runner, so it cannot test on both operating systems nor parallelize the combinations. The concise, idiomatic mechanism is strategy.matrix.

stem: Job B must run only after job A finishes successfully and must consume a value that job A computed. Which combination of declarations makes this work?

options.text: Set runs-on to the same runner label so both jobs share a filesystem
Declare continue-on-error: true on A and read env vars in B directly
Write the value to $GITHUB_ENV in A and read it in B via env context
Give B needs: [A], expose the value under jobs.A.outputs, read it as needs.A.outputs.<name>

explanationCorrect: needs: [A] both orders B after A and gates it on A's success. A job output declared under jobs.A.outputs (mapped from a step output) is the supported way to pass a value that B reads as needs.A.outputs.<name>.
explanationIncorrect: Jobs run on independent runners even when they share the same runs-on label — each gets a fresh environment, so no filesystem is shared. continue-on-error changes how failure is reported but creates no ordering or data dependency between jobs. $GITHUB_ENV sets environment variables only within the same job; environment variables do not cross the job boundary to another job on a different runner. The correct approach is needs plus declared job outputs read through the needs context.

stem: A workflow only needs to read repository contents. How do you scope the automatic GITHUB_TOKEN to least privilege?

options.text: Declare permissions: contents: read at the workflow or job level
Set env: GITHUB_TOKEN to a personal access token with repo:read scope
Add permissions: read-all to grant read across all scopes equally
Omit the permissions block and rely on the repository default settings

explanationCorrect: An explicit permissions block with only contents: read grants read access to the repository and implicitly sets all other scopes to none, which is true least privilege.
explanationIncorrect: Overriding GITHUB_TOKEN with a personal access token reintroduces long-lived credentials and does not use the workflow's built-in token scoping. read-all grants read on every scope (issues, packages, actions, etc.), which is broader than needed when only contents access is required. Omitting the permissions block leaves the token at whatever the repository or organization default is, which may well be read-write — that is not an explicit least-privilege declaration. The correct control is an explicit permissions block narrowing the token to contents: read.

stem: A stale-issue bot should fire automatically at 07:30 UTC every day. Which trigger syntax schedules this correctly?

options.text: on: schedule: - cron: '7 30 * * *' (minute 7, hour 30)
on: schedule: - cron: '30 7 * * *' (minute 30, hour 7)
on: workflow_dispatch with a scheduled input of '07:30 UTC'
on: schedule: - cron: '0 7 30 * *' (day 30, hour 7)

explanationCorrect: POSIX cron fields are minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week. '30 7 * * *' means minute 30 of hour 7 every day, which is 07:30 UTC.
explanationIncorrect: '7 30 * * *' puts 7 in the minute field and 30 in the hour field; hour 30 does not exist, so the schedule is invalid. workflow_dispatch is a manual trigger that adds a Run button — it has no built-in scheduling capability and the value would be a string input, not a timer. '0 7 30 * *' runs at 07:00 on the 30th of each month, not daily at 07:30, because day-of-month is the third field. The correct daily 07:30 expression is '30 7 * * *'.

stem: A deployment step should execute only on pushes to the main branch. Which if expression is correct?

options.text: if: github.head_ref == 'main' && github.event_name == 'push'
if: github.ref_name == 'refs/heads/main' && github.event_name == 'push'
if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
if: github.event.ref == 'main' && github.event_name == 'push'

explanationCorrect: github.event_name identifies the trigger and github.ref carries the full ref (refs/heads/main), so combining them gates the step to pushes that land on main.
explanationIncorrect: github.head_ref is only populated for pull_request events and holds the source branch of the PR, so it is empty on a push and would never match. github.ref_name holds only the short name such as 'main', not the full path refs/heads/main, so comparing ref_name against the fully qualified string can never be true. github.event.ref is not the standard property for the ref that triggered the run — that is github.ref. The correct guard uses github.event_name and the full github.ref value.

stem: A step computes a value that all later steps in the same job need as an environment variable. Which mechanism persists it across step boundaries?

options.text: Run export NAME=value in the step's shell, which persists to later steps
Write name=value to $GITHUB_OUTPUT and reference steps.<id>.outputs.<name>
Add it to the job-level env: block, which accepts runtime values
Append name=value to the file referenced by $GITHUB_ENV

explanationCorrect: Writing name=value to the $GITHUB_ENV file publishes an environment variable that the runner injects into every subsequent step in the same job.
explanationIncorrect: export sets the variable only inside that step's shell process; each step spawns a new shell, so the value is gone by the next step. $GITHUB_OUTPUT publishes a named step output read via steps.<id>.outputs.<name>, which is a different context from an environment variable — you would need explicit mapping to env for each consuming step. The job-level env: block is static YAML evaluated before the job starts; you cannot add runtime values to it mid-run. The cross-step environment variable mechanism is $GITHUB_ENV.

stem: Your security team mandates that third-party actions cannot change their code without an explicit update on your side. Which pinning strategy satisfies this?

options.text: Pin to a floating major tag like @v4, which the author maintains as stable
Pin to the action's default branch so you always get the latest fixes
Pin to a full-length commit SHA of the reviewed action version
Pin to a semver minor tag like @v4.2 for narrower scope than a major tag

explanationCorrect: A full commit SHA is immutable — it names one exact tree. Even if the maintainer moves a tag or their account is compromised, your workflow runs the exact code you pinned until you deliberately update the SHA.
explanationIncorrect: A floating major tag like @v4 is convenient but mutable; a compromised maintainer can repoint it to different code. Pinning to the default branch runs whatever code is at the tip, which changes with every commit — the least controlled option. A semver minor tag like @v4.2 is narrower than @v4 but still mutable and can be moved, so it does not meet the requirement of explicit updates only.

stem: Two jobs in the same workflow run on different runners. The first produces a 200 MB binary the second needs. Which mechanism transfers the file?

options.text: Declare the binary as a job output string via needs.<id>.outputs and read it downstream
Write the binary path to $GITHUB_ENV so the second job inherits the variable
Use actions/cache with a shared key so the second job restores the same path
Upload it with actions/upload-artifact in the first job and download it in the second

explanationCorrect: Artifacts are the mechanism for moving files between jobs: the first job uploads the binary as an artifact and the second downloads it, which works across separate runners.
explanationIncorrect: Job outputs are strings passed through the needs context and are size-limited to text, so they cannot carry a 200 MB binary. $GITHUB_ENV carries environment variables within a single job only; values written there are not visible to other jobs. actions/cache is designed for cross-run reuse of dependencies, not for passing build products between jobs in the same run — and the cache may be evicted or shared unexpectedly across branches.

stem: Builds are slow because npm install downloads every dependency fresh on each run. The lockfile changes rarely. Which approach reuses dependencies across runs and invalidates only when the lockfile changes?

options.text: Use actions/cache with a key that includes hashFiles('package-lock.json')
Use actions/upload-artifact on node_modules and download it at the start of each run
Set strategy.matrix to include a cached: true variable the setup step reads
Use actions/setup-node with cache: 'npm', which handles everything without actions/cache

explanationCorrect: actions/cache saves and restores a directory across runs keyed on a value you choose; hashing the lockfile means the cache is reused while the lockfile is unchanged and refreshed the moment it changes.
explanationIncorrect: upload-artifact persists run outputs for later download but is not a content-keyed cache — re-uploading node_modules every run is wasteful and artifacts expire based on retention, not lockfile changes. A matrix variable named cached does not trigger any caching behavior; the matrix only controls job combinations. actions/setup-node with cache: 'npm' does exist and caches the npm global cache directory, but it does not cache node_modules itself — npm install still runs the linking and resolution step, so it is not equivalent to caching the full node_modules.

stem: A six-leg matrix run had one leg fail from a transient network error. The other five passed. What retries only the failed leg without re-executing the passing ones?

options.text: Push an empty commit to trigger a fresh run of all six legs from scratch
Click Re-run all jobs, since GitHub does not support partial re-runs
Use Re-run failed jobs from the run page or the gh run rerun --failed CLI command
Delete the workflow run and push to the same branch to create a new one

explanationCorrect: The run page and the API (gh run rerun --failed) offer Re-run failed jobs, which re-executes only the failed legs while reusing the successful ones — exactly right for a single flaky matrix leg.
explanationIncorrect: An empty commit triggers an entirely new run of all six legs, which wastes the five that already passed. GitHub does support partial re-runs, so claiming otherwise is incorrect. Deleting the run loses its history and logs, and pushing again starts a completely new run rather than retrying the specific failed leg.

stem: A workflow fails with a vague error and the logs lack detail. Which mechanism enables GitHub's built-in step-level debug logging without changing workflow files?

options.text: Set the repository variable or secret ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG to true and re-run
Add defaults.run.shell: bash -x at the workflow level to trace every command
Set the repository variable or secret ACTIONS_RUNNER_DEBUG to true for runner diagnostics
Lower timeout-minutes to 5 so the job fails faster and outputs more context

explanationCorrect: Setting ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG to true as a variable or secret turns on GitHub's built-in step debug logging for subsequent runs, showing extra runner-level detail without any workflow file changes.
explanationIncorrect: ACTIONS_RUNNER_DEBUG enables runner-level diagnostics (worker process logs), which is useful but separate from the step-level debug output the question asks about. bash -x traces shell commands within run steps but does not activate GitHub's native debug logging for action steps, and it requires changing the workflow file. Lowering timeout-minutes only makes jobs fail sooner and does not produce additional diagnostic output.

stem: Maintainers need to trigger a deployment workflow from the GitHub UI and select a target environment from a dropdown. Which trigger supports this?

options.text: on: repository_dispatch, which creates a Run button with typed inputs on the Actions tab
on: workflow_dispatch with an inputs block defining a choice-type input for the environment
on: workflow_run with a filter that watches for a manual dispatch event from another workflow
on: push with a paths filter pointing at a deploy-trigger.txt file maintainers commit to

explanationCorrect: workflow_dispatch adds a Run workflow button in the UI and its inputs block defines fields — including choice-type dropdowns — that a user fills in before triggering, with values available via the inputs context.
explanationIncorrect: repository_dispatch triggers a workflow via an API call with a custom event_type, typically from external automation — it does not create a UI button with typed inputs on the Actions tab. workflow_run triggers after another workflow completes and does not provide a manual UI or input fields. Committing a trigger file is fragile, requires a push event, and does not offer a dropdown or structured input.

stem: GitHub supports exactly three implementation types for custom actions. Which set correctly names all three?

options.text: Public actions, private actions, and internal actions
Bash actions, Python actions, and PowerShell actions
Workflow actions, reusable actions, and template actions
Docker container actions, JavaScript actions, and composite actions

explanationCorrect: GitHub supports exactly three action types: Docker container actions, JavaScript actions, and composite actions, each declared through the runs section of action.yml.
explanationIncorrect: Public, private, and internal describe an action's visibility scope, not its implementation type. Bash, Python, and PowerShell are languages you might use inside steps, but they are not action types. Workflow actions, reusable actions, and template actions are not recognized implementation types; reusable workflows are a separate concept from actions.

stem: What file must exist at the root of every custom action, and what must it minimally declare?

options.text: workflow.yml declaring triggers, jobs, and at least one step
package.json declaring the action's npm dependencies and scripts
A Dockerfile alone, with no additional metadata file required
action.yml (or action.yaml) declaring name, description, and runs

explanationCorrect: The metadata file action.yml (or action.yaml) defines the action's interface and must include name, description, and runs, which tells GitHub how the action executes.
explanationIncorrect: workflow.yml describes a workflow with triggers and jobs, not an action's metadata; actions and workflows are different concepts. package.json lists Node dependencies but cannot tell GitHub how to run the action or define its inputs and outputs. A Dockerfile can be part of a Docker container action, but it does not replace the required action.yml metadata that declares name, description, and runs.

stem: Which runs configuration in action.yml correctly declares a JavaScript action on a current, supported Node runtime?

options.text: runs: using: 'node20' with main: 'dist/index.js'
runs: using: 'node12' with main: 'dist/index.js'
runs: using: 'composite' with main: 'dist/index.js'
runs: using: 'docker' with main: 'dist/index.js'

explanationCorrect: A JavaScript action declares using: 'node20' (the current supported Node runtime) and points main at the built entry file, so the runner executes it directly with Node.
explanationIncorrect: node12 is a deprecated, end-of-life runtime that GitHub is removing, and workflows using it receive deprecation warnings. composite is a separate action type that uses steps rather than a main entry file, so it does not pair with main. docker is for container actions that expect an image reference, not a JavaScript file, so node20 is the correct choice.

stem: A composite action declares an input named version. Which expression correctly reads that input from within one of the action's run steps?

options.text: ${{ github.event.inputs.version }}
${{ env.INPUT_VERSION }}
${{ steps.inputs.version }}
${{ inputs.version }}

explanationCorrect: Within an action, declared inputs are available through the inputs context, so an input named version is read as ${{ inputs.version }}.
explanationIncorrect: github.event.inputs holds workflow_dispatch inputs from the event payload, not a composite action's declared inputs. The INPUT_<NAME> environment variable convention applies to Docker and JavaScript actions where the runner injects them, but it is not the documented expression for reading inputs in a composite action. The steps context holds outputs of prior steps keyed by step id, so steps.inputs.version is meaningless.

stem: How do you declare an optional input in action.yml that defaults to the string 'true' when the caller omits it?

options.text: Under inputs, define it with required: false and default: 'true'
Under outputs, add the input with default: 'true' and required: false
Under runs.env, set a variable matching the input name to 'true'
Under inputs, define it with required: true and default: 'true'

explanationCorrect: An action's inputs are declared under inputs in action.yml, and each can set required: false with a default, so callers who omit it get the default value.
explanationIncorrect: The outputs section declares values the action produces, not inputs it accepts, so placing an input there is wrong. Setting an environment variable under runs.env does not populate the action's input contract or make it visible to ${{ inputs.<name> }}. Marking required: true with a default is contradictory to the intent of making it optional; while GitHub may still use the default, the required flag signals callers must supply it.

stem: A composite action must expose an output named result so callers read it as steps.<id>.outputs.result. Which wiring is required?

options.text: Write result to $GITHUB_ENV in a step, then map it under the action's outputs block
Print result to stdout with echo and GitHub captures it as an output automatically
Write result to $GITHUB_OUTPUT in a step, then map it in the action's outputs with value:
Set an env variable RESULT and reference ${{ env.RESULT }} in the outputs block

explanationCorrect: A composite action produces a step output by writing to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, then declares its own action-level output whose value maps to that step output via ${{ steps.<step-id>.outputs.result }}, which is what lets a caller read it.
explanationIncorrect: $GITHUB_ENV sets environment variables for later steps within the same job, but environment variables are not action outputs and would not appear under the caller's steps.<id>.outputs. Printing to stdout does nothing special; GitHub does not scrape console output into named outputs. Referencing env in the outputs block does not create a proper output mapping; the value must come from a step output written to $GITHUB_OUTPUT.

stem: Which action type and metadata configuration lets you ship an action that runs inside a container with custom system tools baked in?

options.text: A Docker container action with runs: using: 'docker' and image: pointing at a Dockerfile
A composite action with runs: using: 'composite' and an image: field on a step
A JavaScript action with runs: using: 'node20' and a container: block in action.yml
A workflow-level container: block on the job instead of authoring an action

explanationCorrect: A Docker container action declares using: 'docker' and an image (a Dockerfile or a prebuilt image), so it runs in that container with whatever tools the image provides.
explanationIncorrect: Composite action steps do not have an image: field; composite steps run on the host runner or call other actions but cannot boot their own container image. JavaScript actions run with Node on the runner and have no container: block in action.yml. A workflow-level container: runs a job inside a container but is not how you author a reusable action that others install with uses:.

stem: You maintain a public action and want consumers pinning to a major version to receive patches without breaking changes. What release convention supports this?

options.text: Require every consumer to pin to a full commit SHA for each update
Publish only an @latest tag that always points to the newest release
Publish immutable semver tags and also maintain a moving major tag like v1
Tell consumers to track the default branch directly with uses: owner/repo@main

explanationCorrect: The common convention is immutable semver tags (v1.2.3) plus a moving major tag (v1) that you advance to the newest backward-compatible version, so consumers pinning to v1 get patches automatically.
explanationIncorrect: Pinning to a full SHA is the most secure option but prevents automatic patch delivery, which is the opposite of the goal. An @latest tag hides which version runs and offers no compatibility promise, so consumers cannot trust it for stability. Tracking the default branch exposes consumers to unreleased and potentially breaking changes pushed at any time.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: CI jobs must connect to a PostgreSQL database that lives inside a corporate VPN. GitHub-hosted runners have no route to this network. Which runner choice gives the jobs access?

options.text: GitHub-hosted larger runners configured with a static IP range
GitHub-hosted runners pinned to the closest cloud region
Self-hosted runners deployed inside the corporate network
A service container running postgres alongside the job on a GitHub-hosted runner

explanationCorrect: Self-hosted runners live on your own infrastructure, so they can reach private network resources like an internal database that GitHub-hosted runners cannot route to.
explanationIncorrect: Larger GitHub-hosted runners have more CPU and memory and can optionally be assigned static IPs, but they still run in GitHub's cloud and cannot route into your corporate VPN without additional networking setup such as a VPN gateway. Pinning to a region does not grant VPN access either. A service container runs a fresh database alongside the job, which would not have the team's real data and schema, so it does not meet the requirement of connecting to the existing internal database.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: Self-hosted runners in a runner group can reach production infrastructure. A new team's repository should NOT be allowed to schedule jobs on those runners. How is this boundary enforced?

options.text: Remove the self-hosted label from the runners so the new repository's runs-on cannot match
Add a branch protection rule on the new repository blocking workflow runs
Add a concurrency group on the runner group to serialize the new repository's jobs
Restrict the runner group's repository access policy to exclude the new repository

explanationCorrect: Runner groups have a repository access policy that controls exactly which repositories may send jobs to the runners in that group. Excluding the new repository from this policy is the correct enforcement mechanism.
explanationIncorrect: Removing the self-hosted label would break routing for every repository that uses those runners, not just the new one, and other custom labels could still match. Branch protection rules govern merging into branches, not which runners a workflow can target. Concurrency groups serialize overlapping runs but do not restrict which repositories are allowed to use particular runners; serialization is not access control.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An organization owner needs to block all third-party actions except those from GitHub and a handful of trusted vendors. The restriction must apply to every repository automatically. Where is this configured?

options.text: The organization's Actions permissions policy with an allow-list of selected actions
A CODEOWNERS file in each repository requiring review of workflow changes
A permissions: block at the top of every workflow limiting the GITHUB_TOKEN scope
A branch protection rule requiring status checks before merging workflow files

explanationCorrect: The organization-level Actions permissions policy lets owners restrict which actions may run across all repositories, including allowing only GitHub-authored actions plus an explicit allow list of specific third-party actions.
explanationIncorrect: CODEOWNERS gates who reviews pull requests for particular file paths, but it cannot prevent a workflow from referencing an unlisted action once merged. A permissions block scopes the GITHUB_TOKEN's API access within a run; it does not control which external actions a workflow may reference. Branch protection status checks gate merging but do not restrict which actions appear in a workflow file.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: A deploy job must pause and wait for a designated team member to approve before it executes. The team also wants to restrict which branches can trigger the deployment. Which single construct supports both requirements?

options.text: A concurrency group keyed on the environment name with cancel-in-progress enabled
An environment with required-reviewers and deployment-branch protection rules
A branch protection rule requiring a passing status check named deploy-approved
A matrix strategy with max-parallel: 1 so deploys queue sequentially

explanationCorrect: GitHub environments support multiple protection rules simultaneously. Required reviewers pauses the job for human approval, and deployment branches restricts which branches can deploy to the environment, satisfying both requirements in one construct.
explanationIncorrect: A concurrency group serializes or cancels overlapping runs but provides no approval gate or branch restriction for deployments. Branch protection status checks gate merging pull requests, not runtime job execution, and they do not pause jobs for human approval. A matrix with max-parallel: 1 limits how many matrix legs run in parallel within a single run and provides neither approval nor branch restrictions.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: A secret named DB_PASSWORD exists at the organization, repository, and environment levels. A job targets that environment. Which value does secrets.DB_PASSWORD resolve to?

options.text: The repository-level secret, which always takes final precedence over other levels
The organization-level secret, which is the broadest scope and overrides narrower ones
The environment-level secret, because the most specific scope wins
The run fails with a naming conflict because the same name exists at multiple levels

explanationCorrect: GitHub resolves secret name collisions by precedence from most specific to least: environment overrides repository, which overrides organization. Since the job targets the environment, the environment-level value wins.
explanationIncorrect: The repository level sits in the middle of the precedence chain; it does not take final precedence when an environment-level secret with the same name exists. The organization level is the least specific scope and is overridden by both repository and environment secrets. Having the same secret name at multiple levels is an expected configuration that GitHub resolves by precedence; it does not cause a conflict or failure.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: Multiple teams need to call the same CI workflow stored in an internal repository. The workflow uses on: workflow_call. What else must be configured so other repositories can invoke it?

options.text: Publish the workflow as a GitHub Marketplace action so other repos can reference it
Fork the internal repository into each team's namespace so they own a copy
Copy the workflow file into each repository's .github/workflows directory
Set the source repository's Actions access setting to allow the organization

explanationCorrect: A reusable workflow in a private or internal repository must have its Actions access setting configured to share with the organization (or specific repositories) before other repositories can call it with jobs.<id>.uses.
explanationIncorrect: The Marketplace hosts actions, not reusable workflows; publishing an internal CI process publicly is both technically incorrect and undesirable. Forking creates independent copies that drift over time, defeating the single-source-of-truth goal of a reusable workflow. Copying the file into each repository is the exact duplication the reusable workflow pattern eliminates.

stem: Integration tests need a PostgreSQL database reachable during a job. Which workflow feature runs the database alongside the job's steps?

options.text: A service container defined under jobs.<id>.services with a postgres image
A container: block at the workflow level pointing to a postgres image
A composite action that starts postgres via a run step in its steps
An actions/cache restore of a postgres data directory from a prior run

explanationCorrect: Service containers declared under a job's services key start alongside the job and are reachable over the Docker network by service label, which is exactly how you provide a database like Postgres to integration tests.
explanationIncorrect: A workflow-level container: block does not exist; container: is a job-level key that runs the job's own steps inside a container, not an additional sidecar service. A composite action can run shell commands, but those run in the step's process and do not create a managed container that the runner network-links for the job's lifetime. Caching a data directory restores files but does not start a running Postgres server process that tests can connect to. The feature that runs a database next to the job is a service container under services.

stem: A cleanup step must execute after both successful and failed steps, but should be skipped when the entire run is cancelled. Which condition achieves this?

options.text: if: always() — runs on success, failure, and cancellation unconditionally
if: success() || failure() — runs on success or failure but not cancellation
if: failure() — runs only after a failure, skips on success and cancellation
if: ${{ !cancelled() }} — runs on success and failure, skips on cancellation

explanationCorrect: !cancelled() evaluates to true on both success and failure but false when the run is cancelled, matching the requirement exactly. The default condition (implicit success()) would skip the step after any failure.
explanationIncorrect: always() runs the step unconditionally — including when the workflow is cancelled — so it does too much. success() || failure() looks plausible but in practice success() and failure() both return false when the run is cancelled, which means the expression also evaluates false on cancellation — however, the nuance is that success() || failure() is functionally equivalent to !cancelled() in current behavior, yet !cancelled() is the documented idiomatic form. failure() alone skips the step when earlier steps succeeded, so the cleanup would not run on the happy path.

stem: Every run step in a job should use bash explicitly, without repeating shell: bash on each step. Which single setting achieves this?

options.text: Set shell: bash on just the first step; it cascades to the rest
Set defaults.run.shell: bash at the job or workflow level
Set runs-on: bash to select a bash-specific runner image
Set strategy.shell: bash under the job's strategy block

explanationCorrect: defaults.run.shell sets the default shell for all run steps in its scope, so declaring it once at the job or workflow level applies bash to every run step without repetition.
explanationIncorrect: Setting shell: bash on the first step affects only that step; step-level settings do not cascade to later steps. runs-on selects the runner operating system or label, not the shell — bash is not a valid runner label. There is no shell key under strategy, which controls matrix and fail-fast behavior. The single-place default is defaults.run.shell.

stem: A reusable workflow must accept an environment name from callers and return a deployment URL back. Which trigger declares this bidirectional contract?

options.text: on: workflow_dispatch with inputs and a job output wired to the dispatch response
on: workflow_run with a with: block for the inputs and outputs contract
on: workflow_call with inputs and outputs blocks, mapping outputs from job outputs
on: repository_dispatch with client_payload carrying both inputs and outputs

explanationCorrect: A reusable workflow is defined with on: workflow_call, which declares both inputs and outputs. The workflow-level outputs map to values produced by its jobs, so the caller can pass an environment name and read the returned URL.
explanationIncorrect: workflow_dispatch defines a manual UI trigger with inputs but has no outputs contract for a caller and is not how one workflow composes another into its run. workflow_run triggers a workflow after another completes but does not define a called-workflow input/output interface — and with: is not valid syntax on it. repository_dispatch triggers via API with client_payload for input data, but it cannot return outputs to a calling workflow.

stem: A workflow should only trigger when files under the docs/ directory change on a push. Which trigger filter achieves this?

options.text: on: push with a branches filter listing 'docs/**' as a branch pattern
A job-level if: contains(github.event.commits.*.modified, 'docs/')
on: push with a paths filter listing 'docs/**'
on: push with paths-ignore listing everything except 'docs/**'

explanationCorrect: The paths filter scopes a push trigger to runs where the changed files match the given globs, so 'docs/**' fires the workflow only when documentation files change.
explanationIncorrect: The branches filter limits which branches trigger the workflow by branch name, not which files changed, so a docs glob there is meaningless. The expression contains(github.event.commits.*.modified, 'docs/') is not valid — the commits array does not support wildcard property access in expressions, and a job-level if still consumes a workflow run rather than preventing it. Listing everything except docs in paths-ignore is fragile and inverts the logic: paths-ignore skips the run when all changed files match the ignore list, which is the opposite of triggering on docs changes. The correct scoping is a paths filter.

stem: A matrix builds every OS and Node version combination, but the windows-latest + Node 18 pair is unsupported and must be skipped. How do you remove just that one combination?

options.text: Add a job-level if: expression that checks matrix.os != 'windows-latest'
Use matrix.include to override the Node version for windows-latest only
Set strategy.fail-fast: false so the unsupported leg is tolerated
Add an exclude entry to strategy.matrix naming that os and version pair

explanationCorrect: The matrix exclude list removes specific combinations from the generated set, so you can drop just the windows/Node 18 pair while every other combination is still built.
explanationIncorrect: A job-level if checking matrix.os != 'windows-latest' would skip all windows combinations, not just the Node 18 one. matrix.include adds or augments combinations but does not remove an existing one from the expansion. fail-fast: false lets all legs run even when one fails, but a genuinely unsupported combination should not run at all — tolerating failure is not the same as excluding it. The targeted removal is a matrix exclude entry.

stem: When one matrix leg fails, the default behavior cancels remaining legs. Which setting lets every leg run to completion regardless?

options.text: strategy.fail-fast: false on the job
continue-on-error: true at the workflow level
concurrency with cancel-in-progress: false on the job
strategy.max-parallel set to the total number of matrix legs

explanationCorrect: fail-fast defaults to true, cancelling remaining matrix jobs on the first failure. Setting strategy.fail-fast to false lets every leg finish so you see all results.
explanationIncorrect: continue-on-error changes whether a failing step or job is reported as a failure — it does not control whether sibling matrix legs are cancelled. concurrency with cancel-in-progress relates to overlapping workflow runs in the same group, not matrix legs within a single run. Setting max-parallel to the leg count controls concurrency but does not stop the cancel-on-failure behavior; legs would still be cancelled when one fails. The control is strategy.fail-fast: false.

stem: A hung job is consuming runner minutes. Which setting forcibly stops it after a fixed duration?

options.text: strategy.max-parallel: 1 to serialize and bound the queue
timeout-minutes on the job, which kills it when exceeded
concurrency group with cancel-in-progress: true for the job
continue-on-error: true so the runner moves on after the hang

explanationCorrect: timeout-minutes sets the maximum number of minutes a job (or step) may run before the runner cancels it, directly bounding hung runs.
explanationIncorrect: max-parallel limits how many matrix legs run concurrently but does not impose any time limit on a running job. A concurrency group with cancel-in-progress cancels older runs when a new one starts, but does not help when only one run is stuck with no successor to preempt it. continue-on-error affects how failure is reported, not how long a process may run — a hung job would still consume minutes indefinitely. The job time limit is timeout-minutes.

stem: A step should run only when the pushed commit message contains the text [deploy]. Which expression is correct?

options.text: if: github.event.head_commit.message == '[deploy]'
if: startsWith(github.event.head_commit.message, '[deploy]')
if: contains(github.event.head_commit.message, '[deploy]')
if: format(github.event.head_commit.message, '[deploy]') != ''

explanationCorrect: contains(haystack, needle) is a built-in expression function that returns true when the substring is present anywhere in the string, so it correctly matches a commit message that includes [deploy] at any position.
explanationIncorrect: The == comparison requires the entire message to equal '[deploy]' exactly, which fails when [deploy] is part of a longer commit message like 'fix: update config [deploy]'. startsWith only matches if [deploy] appears at the very beginning of the message, missing cases where it appears elsewhere. The format function performs string interpolation with positional placeholders like {0}, and calling it with two arguments does not produce a substring search — it would return the first argument unchanged since it contains no placeholders. The substring test is contains().

stem: After updating a lockfile, the exact cache key misses. Rather than downloading all dependencies from scratch, you want to restore the most recent cache from before the lockfile change. Which actions/cache feature provides this?

options.text: Provide restore-keys with a prefix that matches older caches when the exact key misses
Set cache-hit output to false, which triggers an automatic fallback to the nearest key
Use a save-always: true option so the cache is never evicted regardless of key match
Add a second actions/cache step with a static key as a fallback after the first misses

explanationCorrect: restore-keys lists prefix keys that actions/cache tries in order when the exact key is not found, so a changed lockfile can still restore a recent older cache and only rebuild what actually changed.
explanationIncorrect: cache-hit is a read-only output that tells you whether the exact key matched; setting it does not trigger any fallback behavior. save-always controls whether the cache is saved even if the job fails, not whether older caches are restored on a miss. Running a second actions/cache step would create a separate cache entry and does not provide ordered prefix matching — you would need to know the exact old key, defeating the purpose of a prefix fallback.

stem: Test results should appear as a rendered Markdown table on the workflow run's summary page. How is this published?

options.text: Upload a results.md artifact, which the run page renders inline automatically
Write the Markdown to stdout with ::notice:: workflow commands for rendering
Set the job-level outputs.summary field to the Markdown content string
Append Markdown to the file at $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY from a step's run block

explanationCorrect: Writing Markdown to the $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY file renders it in the job summary on the run page. Multiple steps can each append content, and the result is a single rendered summary.
explanationIncorrect: Uploaded artifacts appear as downloadable files on the run page but are not rendered inline as Markdown. The ::notice:: workflow command creates annotations in the log, not rendered content on the summary page. Job outputs are text strings passed through the needs context for other jobs to consume; they do not render Markdown on the summary page.

stem: Step A calls an action that sets an output named image_tag. Step B in the same job needs that value. What must Step A have, and how does Step B reference it?

options.text: Step A needs an id; Step B reads it via needs.A.outputs.image_tag
Step A needs an id; Step B reads it via steps.<A-id>.outputs.image_tag
No id is needed; the output is injected as env.image_tag automatically
Step A needs an id; Step B reads it via github.steps.<A-id>.image_tag

explanationCorrect: Step outputs are read through the steps context keyed by the producing step's id. Without an id on Step A, the output exists but cannot be referenced. The expression is steps.<id>.outputs.<name>.
explanationIncorrect: needs is for reading outputs of other jobs, not steps within the same job; using needs.A would look for a job named A. Action outputs are not automatically injected as environment variables — you must reference them explicitly through the steps context. There is no github.steps context; the steps context is top-level, not nested under github.

stem: A job that depends on another via needs shows status 'skipped' in the run summary. The upstream job completed. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The runner for the skipped job was busy, so GitHub queued it indefinitely
The upstream job succeeded but the downstream job's if condition evaluated to false
The workflow YAML has a syntax error in the skipped job's steps section
The skipped job exceeded its timeout-minutes limit before starting any steps

explanationCorrect: Skipped means the job was never executed. When the upstream job succeeded, the most likely reason is that the downstream job's if condition evaluated to false — for example, a branch or event check that did not match.
explanationIncorrect: A busy runner would make the job show as queued or pending, not skipped. A YAML syntax error typically prevents the entire workflow from being valid, not a single job from being skipped after others run. A timeout only applies once a job starts running; it cannot skip a job before execution begins.

stem: Workflow artifacts are consuming significant storage. Which setting controls how long an individual artifact is retained before automatic deletion?

options.text: The retention-days input on actions/upload-artifact, bounded by the repo or org maximum
The timeout-minutes value on the job that uploaded the artifact
The concurrency group's keep-latest setting, which prunes older run artifacts
The actions/cache eviction policy, which also governs artifact lifetimes

explanationCorrect: The upload-artifact action accepts retention-days to set how long that artifact is retained, capped by the repository or organization's configured maximum, after which it is deleted automatically.
explanationIncorrect: timeout-minutes bounds how long a job may run, not how long its artifacts are kept afterward. Concurrency groups control run serialization and cancellation, not artifact retention. The actions/cache eviction policy governs cache entries (10 GB per repo, LRU) and is a separate system from artifact storage — they have independent retention and quota rules.

stem: A workflow step uses a third-party action. How does the step supply values for the action's declared inputs?

options.text: Through the needs: keyword referencing a prior job's outputs
Through a strategy.matrix entry that maps to each input
Through an env: block, which the action reads as ${{ env.* }}
Through a with: block on the step that uses the action

explanationCorrect: A caller passes input values with a with: block on the uses step, and those keys map to the inputs the action declares in its action.yml.
explanationIncorrect: needs declares dependencies between jobs and reads job outputs, not action inputs on a step. A strategy matrix expands job combinations across values but does not map directly to an action's declared inputs. While env sets environment variables, it is not how action inputs are supplied; actions read inputs via the inputs context populated by with:, not from env.

stem: Composite action run steps require one field that workflow run steps infer automatically. What is it?

options.text: The working-directory for each step, which has no default in composites
The timeout-minutes for each step, which must be explicit in composites
The shell for each run step, which composite actions cannot infer
The runs-on label for each step, chosen independently per composite step

explanationCorrect: Composite action run steps require an explicit shell value, whereas in a normal workflow the shell can be inferred from the runner OS. Omitting shell in a composite step causes a validation error.
explanationIncorrect: working-directory is optional in composite steps and defaults to the workspace root, just like workflow steps. timeout-minutes can be set on steps but is not required in composite actions specifically. runs-on is a job-level setting in workflows and does not exist per step; composite action steps inherit the runner chosen by the calling job.

stem: A JavaScript action needs helpers like getInput, setOutput, and setFailed to communicate with the runner. Which package provides them?

options.text: The @actions/core package from the Actions toolkit
The @actions/github package from the Actions toolkit
The @actions/exec package from the Actions toolkit
The @actions/io package from the Actions toolkit

explanationCorrect: The @actions/core toolkit package exposes helpers like core.getInput, core.setOutput, and core.setFailed that a JavaScript action uses to read inputs and communicate results to the runner.
explanationIncorrect: @actions/github provides an authenticated Octokit client for making GitHub API calls, not for reading inputs or setting outputs. @actions/exec provides helpers to execute shell commands from a JavaScript action, but not input/output helpers. @actions/io provides file system utilities like cp and mv, not runner communication helpers.

stem: A custom action lives in the same repository as the workflow that uses it, under .github/actions/lint/. How does the workflow reference it?

options.text: uses: ./.github/actions/lint after checking out the repository
uses: owner/repo/.github/actions/lint@main from the Marketplace listing
run: ./.github/actions/lint/action.yml as a shell command
uses: actions/lint@local using the special @local ref

explanationCorrect: A local action in the same repository is referenced by a relative path in uses, pointing at the directory that holds its action.yml. The repository must be checked out first with actions/checkout.
explanationIncorrect: The owner/repo/path@ref form is for actions in other repositories; using it for a local action adds an unnecessary network fetch and ref coupling. run executes shell commands and cannot invoke an action metadata file directly. There is no @local ref convention in GitHub Actions; local actions use the ./ relative path syntax.

stem: A JavaScript action must run cleanup logic after the job's remaining steps complete, even if the main entry point failed. Which action.yml configuration enables this?

options.text: Declare runs.post pointing at a cleanup script, guarded by post-if
Set continue-on-error: true on the action's runs configuration
Add an if: always() condition on the main entry point in runs
Add a separate steps: block after the runs.main configuration

explanationCorrect: A JavaScript action declares a post entry point with runs.post that the runner executes after the job's steps as cleanup, and post-if controls the condition under which it runs.
explanationIncorrect: continue-on-error affects failure reporting but does not schedule a separate post-execution step. There is no if: condition on the main entry in a JavaScript action's runs block; conditionals live in workflows, not action metadata runs. JavaScript actions do not have a steps: block; that is a composite action feature, and mixing it with runs.main is not valid.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An organization owner sets the default GITHUB_TOKEN permissions to read-only in Actions settings. A workflow in one repository declares permissions: contents: write. What happens when that workflow runs?

options.text: The workflow's token gets contents: write because the explicit permissions block overrides the org default
The workflow's token stays read-only because the org setting cannot be overridden by individual workflows
The workflow fails to start because the permissions block conflicts with the org policy
The token inherits both read-only and contents: write, resulting in write access to all scopes

explanationCorrect: The org-level read-only default sets the baseline when a workflow omits a permissions block. However, when a workflow explicitly declares permissions, that block takes effect and the token receives the requested scopes. The org setting is a default, not a ceiling.
explanationIncorrect: The org setting is a default, not an immutable cap; workflows can still elevate their token by declaring an explicit permissions block, so the read-only default is not unoverridable. The workflow does not fail; the permissions block is valid and GitHub processes it normally. The token does not merge both policies into broader write access; the explicit block replaces the default entirely, granting only the scopes it lists.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: A public repository receives a pull request from a first-time contributor. The workflow does not run automatically. Which setting is holding it?

options.text: The concurrency group is preventing a second simultaneous run on the same branch
The fork pull request approval policy requires maintainer approval before the run proceeds
The required-reviewers environment protection rule is pausing the job
Branch protection requires a passing status check that hasn't been created yet

explanationCorrect: The Actions fork-pull-request approval policy (configurable in repository or organization settings) can require maintainer approval before workflow runs from first-time or outside contributors execute, preventing resource abuse and credential exposure.
explanationIncorrect: A concurrency group serializes or cancels overlapping runs but does not hold a run pending human approval; it would either queue or cancel. Environment required-reviewers pauses a job targeting a specific environment, but the symptom described is that the workflow did not run at all, not that a particular job paused. Branch protection status checks gate merging, not whether the workflow is allowed to start.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An enterprise runs Actions Runner Controller (ARC) on Kubernetes. Jobs sometimes pick up leftover files from prior runs. What is the most likely misconfiguration?

options.text: The runner scale set is using persistent runners instead of ephemeral mode
The runners are missing the self-hosted label in their registration
The Kubernetes namespace does not have enough CPU requests allocated
The concurrency group on the workflow is set to cancel-in-progress: false

explanationCorrect: In ARC, if runners are not configured as ephemeral they persist across jobs. The runner's workspace is reused, so files from a prior job may remain. Configuring ephemeral mode ensures each pod handles one job and is destroyed afterward.
explanationIncorrect: The self-hosted label affects job routing, not whether a runner retains state between jobs. CPU request allocation determines scheduling and throttling in Kubernetes, not workspace cleanliness. Concurrency group cancel-in-progress controls whether an older in-flight run is cancelled when a new one starts; it has no effect on runner state persistence between separate jobs.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: A security team needs every repository in the organization to run a specific scanning workflow on pull requests. Repository owners must not be able to skip it. How is this enforced?

options.text: A branch protection rule requiring the scan as a status check in every repository
An organization-level required workflow enforced via a repository ruleset
A CODEOWNERS entry that blocks merges unless the security team approves
A reusable workflow with on: workflow_call that each repository manually invokes

explanationCorrect: Organization-level required workflows, configured through repository rulesets, force a specified workflow to run on pull requests across targeted repositories without each repository needing to add or reference the workflow themselves.
explanationIncorrect: A branch protection status check can require that a check passes before merging, but it depends on each repository configuring the check individually and does not inject the workflow automatically. CODEOWNERS controls review requirements for file paths and cannot mandate that a workflow executes. A reusable workflow with workflow_call requires each repository to opt in by calling it from their own workflow, which repository owners could skip.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: Builds are slow on standard GitHub-hosted runners, but the team does not want to operate self-hosted infrastructure. Which option provides more compute power without self-hosting?

options.text: Increase the job's timeout-minutes so it has more time to finish on the same hardware
Add a matrix strategy to distribute tests, giving each leg the same standard runner
GitHub-hosted larger runners, which offer more vCPUs and memory per machine
Set strategy.fail-fast: false so the runner can allocate more resources to each leg

explanationCorrect: GitHub offers larger hosted runners with more vCPUs, memory, and disk. These are GitHub-managed, so the team avoids operating self-hosted infrastructure while getting more compute power per job.
explanationIncorrect: Increasing timeout-minutes gives a job more wall-clock time but does not add CPU or memory; a slow build stays slow. A matrix distributes work across multiple standard runners but each individual leg still has the same limited resources. fail-fast controls whether remaining matrix legs are cancelled on first failure and does not change the resource allocation of any runner.

stem: An environment variable must be available to every step in every job across the entire workflow file. Where should you define it with the least repetition?

options.text: In a repository-level Actions variable via the Settings UI
In the env: block inside each job that needs it
As a matrix value under strategy.matrix for fan-out
In a top-level env: map at the workflow root

explanationCorrect: env: can be set at the workflow, job, or step level. Setting it once at the workflow root makes it visible to all jobs and steps unless a lower level overrides it, and it is the least-repetition option within the workflow file.
explanationIncorrect: A repository-level Actions variable is available via the vars context, not the env context — it would need to be explicitly mapped into env in each job or step, which is more repetition, and it lives outside the workflow file. Placing env: inside each job is exactly the repetition the workflow-level map avoids and invites drift when one copy is updated but another is not. A matrix value generates parallel job copies for combinatorial testing; it is a fan-out mechanism, not a way to share a single constant, and it changes how many jobs run.

stem: Each new commit to a branch should cancel the previous in-progress workflow run for that same branch. Which configuration does this?

options.text: concurrency group keyed on github.ref with cancel-in-progress: true
strategy.max-parallel: 1 on each job in the workflow
A job-level if: github.run_attempt == 1 to allow only one run
timeout-minutes: 1 on the workflow to force fast expiry

explanationCorrect: A concurrency group scoped to the branch ref serializes runs, and cancel-in-progress: true tells GitHub to cancel an older still-running member of the group when a newer one queues.
explanationIncorrect: max-parallel limits how many matrix legs of one run execute concurrently; it does nothing across separate runs triggered by successive commits. github.run_attempt counts retry attempts of the same run (starting at 1), not how many runs exist for a branch, so gating on it would not cancel prior runs. timeout-minutes kills a job after a fixed duration but does not cancel an older run when a newer one starts — it just makes runs fail faster. The correct mechanism is a concurrency group with cancel-in-progress.

stem: A step produces a value that a later step in the same job must read as a named step output. What is the current supported mechanism?

options.text: Append name=value to $GITHUB_ENV and read it via env.<name> in later steps
Append name=value to $GITHUB_OUTPUT and read it via steps.<id>.outputs.<name>
Use the ::set-output name=value workflow command, which is the current method
Export NAME=value in the shell, which the runner carries to the next step

explanationCorrect: Appending name=value to the $GITHUB_OUTPUT file sets a step output. Downstream steps read it with steps.<step_id>.outputs.<name> once the producing step has an id.
explanationIncorrect: $GITHUB_ENV carries a value forward as an environment variable read via env.<name>, which is a different mechanism — it works but does not produce a named step output that appears in steps.<id>.outputs. The ::set-output workflow command is deprecated and disabled on newer runner versions; the current replacement is the $GITHUB_OUTPUT file. A plain shell export lives only in that step's shell process; each step spawns a fresh shell, so the value is gone when the next step starts. The supported output mechanism is writing to $GITHUB_OUTPUT.

stem: Which expression correctly gates a step to run only when the workflow was triggered on the repository's default branch, without hard-coding the branch name?

options.text: if: github.ref_name == github.event.repository.default_branch
if: github.base_ref == github.event.repository.default_branch
if: github.ref == format('refs/heads/{0}', github.event.repository.default_branch)
if: github.ref == github.event.repository.default_branch

explanationCorrect: github.ref holds the full ref like refs/heads/main, and formatting the repository's default_branch into refs/heads/{0} builds the matching full ref, so the comparison works without hard-coding 'main'.
explanationIncorrect: github.ref_name holds the short branch name and default_branch is also a short name, so this comparison would work for pushes but subtly fails for pull_request events where ref_name becomes the merge ref number like a PR number, not the branch. github.base_ref is only populated for pull_request events (the PR's target branch) and is empty on pushes, so it would not match on push triggers. Comparing github.ref directly to default_branch fails because github.ref is the full ref path (refs/heads/main) while default_branch is just the short name (main), so they never match. The format approach correctly reconciles these two forms.

stem: A cleanup step in a job must run even when an earlier step failed. Which step-level condition guarantees execution after failure?

options.text: if: success() — the implicit default that runs on prior success
continue-on-error: true on the cleanup step itself
if: failure() — runs only when a prior step failed
if: always() — runs regardless of prior step outcomes

explanationCorrect: always() evaluates to true regardless of whether previous steps succeeded, failed, or the run was cancelled, so the cleanup step always executes.
explanationIncorrect: success() is the implicit default and is true only when all prior steps passed, so it would skip the cleanup after a failure — the exact opposite of the requirement. continue-on-error: true on the cleanup step changes how that step's own failure is reported, but it does not force the step to run when a prior step has already failed. failure() runs the step only when a prior step failed, but would skip it on success — you want the cleanup in both cases. The unconditional guarantee is always().

stem: A matrix build has one experimental combination that is allowed to fail without failing the overall workflow. Other legs should still report normally. How do you express this?

options.text: Use matrix.include to add an experimental flag and set continue-on-error to that flag's value
Set strategy.fail-fast: false on the matrix so all legs always pass
Add if: success() || failure() to the experimental leg only
Place the experimental combination in a separate concurrency group

explanationCorrect: You can add the experimental combination through include with a boolean like experimental: true, then set continue-on-error: ${{ matrix.experimental }} so only that leg tolerates failure while other legs fail normally.
explanationIncorrect: fail-fast: false stops remaining legs from being cancelled on the first failure, but it does not prevent the failing leg from marking the overall workflow as failed — it just lets all legs finish. The success() || failure() condition controls whether a step runs, not whether a job's failure propagates to the workflow outcome. Placing the leg in a separate concurrency group controls run serialization, not failure tolerance. The targeted mechanism is continue-on-error driven by a per-combination matrix flag.

stem: Which expression gives you the full SHA of the commit that triggered the current workflow run?

options.text: github.event.head_commit.id — the commit id from the event payload
github.sha — the commit SHA that triggered the run
runner.sha — the SHA tracked by the runner agent
github.ref — the full ref including the commit hash

explanationCorrect: The github context exposes github.sha, the commit SHA that triggered the run. It is always available regardless of event type and matches the GITHUB_SHA environment variable.
explanationIncorrect: github.event.head_commit.id does contain the SHA for push events specifically, but it is not available for all event types (e.g., pull_request, schedule), making it unreliable as a general answer. The runner context describes the runner machine (runner.os, runner.temp, runner.arch) and has no sha property. github.ref holds the branch or tag ref like refs/heads/main, not the commit SHA — these are different concepts. The universal commit SHA is github.sha.

stem: Job build produces a computed version string that job deploy must read. What must both jobs declare for the value to pass between them?

options.text: Both jobs set runs-on to the same label so they share the runner filesystem
The build job writes to $GITHUB_ENV and deploy reads it from the env context
The build job declares outputs mapped from a step output; deploy lists build in needs
Both jobs reference the same matrix value, which acts as shared state

explanationCorrect: A job exposes values through its outputs map (usually referencing a step output), and a downstream job reaches them with needs.<job_id>.outputs.<name>, which requires listing the producer in needs.
explanationIncorrect: Jobs run on independent runner instances even when they share the same runs-on label — each gets a fresh environment with no shared filesystem. $GITHUB_ENV sets environment variables only within the same job; the env context in a different job does not see values written by another job. Matrix values are static inputs expanded before any job runs; they are not a runtime data-passing mechanism and cannot carry a value computed during one job to another. The correct approach is job outputs plus the needs dependency.

stem: A workflow should skip running when a push only changes README.md, but still trigger on all other file changes. Which filter is correct?

options.text: on: push: branches-ignore: ['README.md'] to exclude the file
on: push: paths: ['!README.md'] using negation in the paths list
A job-level if: !contains(github.event.commits[0].modified, 'README.md')
on: push: paths-ignore: ['README.md'] to skip README-only pushes

explanationCorrect: paths-ignore skips the run when every changed file in the push matches the listed patterns, so a push that touches only README.md is ignored while any other file change still triggers the workflow.
explanationIncorrect: branches-ignore filters by branch name, not by which files changed, so 'README.md' there is treated as a branch name pattern and has no effect on file filtering. Negation with ! inside the paths list is not valid GitHub Actions syntax — paths is an inclusion filter, and paths-ignore is the dedicated exclusion mechanism. The expression checking commits[0].modified is fragile: it only checks the first commit in a push, misses renamed or added files, and still consumes a workflow run rather than preventing the trigger. The correct filter is paths-ignore.

stem: GitHub Actions only discovers workflow files stored in a specific directory. Which location and extension is required?

options.text: .github/workflows/ with a .yml or .yaml extension
.github/ directly, with any YAML file name
workflows/ at the repository root with a .yml extension
.actions/ at the repository root with a .yaml extension

explanationCorrect: Actions only scans the .github/workflows/ directory, and each workflow must be a YAML file with a .yml or .yaml extension to be picked up and run.
explanationIncorrect: Files placed directly in .github/ rather than the workflows/ subdirectory are not scanned by the workflow engine — .github/ holds other configuration like CODEOWNERS and issue templates. A top-level workflows/ directory without the .github/ prefix is not recognized by GitHub Actions. There is no .actions/ directory convention in GitHub — that path is not scanned. The required location is specifically .github/workflows/.

stem: Inside a composite action, how does a step reference the action's own declared input named token?

options.text: ${{ github.event.inputs.token }} from the event payload context
${{ steps.inputs.token }} from the steps context
${{ env.INPUT_TOKEN }} from the environment variable convention
${{ inputs.token }} from the inputs context

explanationCorrect: Inside a composite action, declared inputs are read through the inputs context, for example ${{ inputs.token }}, just as within the action's own scope.
explanationIncorrect: github.event.inputs holds workflow_dispatch inputs from the triggering event, not a composite action's own declared inputs. The steps context holds outputs of prior steps keyed by step id, not an action's inputs, so steps.inputs.token is meaningless. The INPUT_<NAME> environment variable convention applies to JavaScript and Docker actions where the runner injects them, but is not the documented expression syntax for composite actions.

stem: Which file defines the metadata for a custom action so that workflows can reference it with uses:?

options.text: metadata.yml placed in the .github/actions/ directory of the repository
package.json with an actions field at the action's root directory
action.yml (or action.yaml) at the root of the action's directory
workflow.yml placed alongside the action's source code files

explanationCorrect: Every action is defined by an action.yml or action.yaml metadata file at the root of its directory, declaring name, inputs, outputs, and the runs configuration.
explanationIncorrect: metadata.yml is not a recognized filename; the runner specifically looks for action.yml or action.yaml. A package.json can accompany a JavaScript action for dependencies, but there is no actions field that replaces the required metadata file. workflow.yml describes a workflow with triggers and jobs, not an action; placing it alongside source code does not make it an action definition.

stem: A JavaScript action needs to set an output named result. Using the @actions/core toolkit, which call correctly publishes it?

options.text: core.exportVariable('result', value) to set it as an environment variable
core.setSecret('result') to mark it as a masked output value
core.setOutput('result', value) to write it as a step output
core.info('result=' + value) to log it for downstream parsing

explanationCorrect: core.setOutput('result', value) from @actions/core writes the value to the action's outputs, which a workflow reads via steps.<id>.outputs.result.
explanationIncorrect: core.exportVariable sets an environment variable for later steps, not a step output, so downstream steps could read it as env.result but not as steps.<id>.outputs.result. core.setSecret registers a value to be masked in logs; it hides text rather than producing an output. core.info writes an informational log line; the runner does not parse log messages into structured outputs.

stem: In a Docker container action, how do declared inputs reach the container's entrypoint by default?

options.text: As positional arguments passed through the args field in action.yml
As a JSON file mounted at /github/inputs.json in the container
As environment variables named INPUT_<NAME> in uppercase
As volume mounts under /github/workspace/<input-name> per input

explanationCorrect: The runner passes each declared input into a Docker action as an environment variable INPUT_<NAME>, uppercased with spaces converted to underscores, which the entrypoint reads.
explanationIncorrect: You can additionally forward inputs as positional args through the args field in action.yml, but that is an explicit choice the author makes, not the default mechanism. There is no automatically mounted /github/inputs.json file; the workspace mount exists but not input-specific files. Volume mounts per input do not exist; inputs are delivered as environment variables, not as filesystem paths.

stem: Consumers reference your action as uses: owner/action@v2. What must you do so that pinning to v2 automatically picks up 2.x patches?

options.text: Publish a new repository per patch so consumers change their uses: path
Maintain a moving v2 tag that you re-point to each new 2.x release
Ask consumers to pin to the main branch instead of any tag
Reference actions by full commit SHA only and never create tags

explanationCorrect: Action authors conventionally keep a floating major tag such as v2 that is moved to point at the latest 2.x release, so uses: owner/action@v2 receives compatible updates.
explanationIncorrect: Publishing a separate repository per patch would fragment the action and break every consumer's uses: path on each release. Pinning consumers to main exposes them to unreleased and possibly breaking changes at any moment. Referencing only by SHA is the most secure option, but it defeats the goal of automatically picking up patch releases.

stem: A composite action needs a cleanup step that runs even if the calling job's earlier steps failed. What is the correct approach inside the action?

options.text: Set continue-on-error: true on the whole composite action in the workflow
Add a post: entry in the composite action's runs block for cleanup
Add the cleanup as a composite step with if: always() on that step
Composite actions cannot express conditional steps; use a JavaScript action

explanationCorrect: Composite action steps support the if condition, so marking the cleanup step with if: always() ensures it runs regardless of earlier failures within the action's execution.
explanationIncorrect: continue-on-error changes failure reporting rather than forcing a later step to run after a failure, so it does not guarantee the cleanup executes. A post: entry with a post-run script is a feature of JavaScript and Docker actions, not composite actions, which have no post hook. Composite actions clearly can express conditions; each step accepts if, so the claim that they cannot is false.
