stem: Why do JavaScript action authors commit a bundled dist/ folder rather than shipping raw source with a separate node_modules directory?

options.text: Bundling is required to list the action on the GitHub Marketplace
The runner does not run npm install for the action, so dependencies must be bundled
Tags cannot reference source files, only pre-compiled dist/ output
GitHub requires all actions to be minified before they can execute

explanationCorrect: When a workflow uses a JavaScript action, the runner checks out the action and runs the entry file directly without running npm install, so authors bundle dependencies (often with ncc) into a committed dist/ file.
explanationIncorrect: Bundling is not a Marketplace requirement; unpublished local actions also need bundling because the runner skips npm install regardless. Tags reference whatever is committed including source files, so the claim they cannot is wrong. There is no rule that actions be minified; bundling is about self-contained dependencies, and the output is still readable JavaScript.

stem: How do you declare that an action produces an output named url in its action.yml metadata?

options.text: Under inputs:, add url: with required: false to make it bidirectional
Under outputs:, add url: with a description and value mapping
Outputs are inferred automatically from $GITHUB_OUTPUT and need no declaration
Under runs:, add env: url: to inject it as an environment variable

explanationCorrect: Action outputs are declared under the outputs: key with a description; a composite action also sets value: to map the output from a step, so consumers can read steps.<id>.outputs.url.
explanationIncorrect: Declaring url under inputs makes it a parameter the caller supplies, not something the action produces; inputs and outputs are separate concepts. Outputs are not inferred automatically; they must be declared in metadata so consumers have a documented contract to rely on. Adding env in the runs block sets environment variables, which is unrelated to declaring an output that callers can reference.

stem: A JavaScript action allocates a temporary cloud resource during main execution and must tear it down after the job finishes. Which metadata configuration handles this?

options.text: Add a needs: dependency on a separate cleanup job in the action
Set runs.after: 'cleanup.js' to run a second script sequentially
Add if: always() to the main entry point in the runs block
Set runs.post: 'cleanup.js' with an optional post-if condition

explanationCorrect: JavaScript actions can declare a post: script in runs that the runner executes at the end of the job, with post-if controlling when it runs, ideal for teardown of resources the action created.
explanationIncorrect: needs expresses dependencies between workflow jobs; actions do not contain jobs or use needs internally. There is no after: key in the runs schema; the post-execution hook is called post. The if: condition is not available on the main entry point in a JavaScript action's runs block; conditionals on steps are a workflow or composite action concept.

stem: What happens when a caller omits an input that has a default: value set in the action's metadata?

options.text: The action receives the default value as if the caller had supplied it
The action fails because required inputs must always be provided
The input is set to an empty string, ignoring the default entirely
The action skips all steps that reference the omitted input

explanationCorrect: An input's default supplies the value the action uses whenever the caller omits that input, giving sensible behavior without requiring every consumer to set it.
explanationIncorrect: An input with a default does not require explicit provision; required: true is a separate field that controls whether omission is an error. The default is not ignored; it is specifically used when the caller omits the input, not replaced by an empty string. Steps referencing the input are not skipped; they receive the default value and execute normally.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: A runner is registered at the organization level and placed in the Default runner group. A newly created repository cannot target it with runs-on. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The workflow is missing the self-hosted label in its runs-on array
The runner group's repository access is set to selected repositories and the new repo is not included
Organization-level runners are always limited to public repositories only
The runner's registration token has expired and must be rotated

explanationCorrect: Even the Default runner group has a repository access policy. If it is set to selected repositories rather than all repositories, a new repo must be explicitly added before its workflows can target those runners.
explanationIncorrect: Missing the self-hosted label in runs-on would affect routing, but the question states the repository cannot target the runner at all, which points to an access issue rather than a label mismatch. Organization-level runners work with both public and private repositories. The registration token is used only during initial registration and does not affect ongoing job scheduling once the runner is connected.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: A self-hosted runner is registered with the labels self-hosted, linux, and gpu. Which runs-on value targets it specifically?

options.text: runs-on: gpu (matches any runner with that single label)
runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, gpu] (requires all three labels to match)
runs-on: self-hosted/gpu (slash-separated path to the runner)
uses: self-hosted/gpu (references the runner as an action)

explanationCorrect: When runs-on is an array, the runner must carry every listed label. Specifying [self-hosted, linux, gpu] ensures the job lands only on a Linux self-hosted runner with the gpu label, targeting it precisely.
explanationIncorrect: Using just gpu would match any runner with that label, including a potential GitHub-hosted larger runner if one happened to carry that label, so it is less specific than the three-label combination. There is no slash-separated path syntax for runs-on; labels are matched as a flat set. uses: references actions or reusable workflows, not runners.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An organization wants to offer a standardized CI template that any member repository can adopt from the Actions tab with one click. Where must the template files be placed?

options.text: In a required-workflows directory of any repository within the organization
In a starter-workflows branch on the target repository's default branch
In the workflow-templates directory of the organization's .github repository
In the organization's wiki under a page named Workflow Templates

explanationCorrect: Organization-level starter workflow templates must be placed in the workflow-templates directory of the special .github repository owned by the organization, along with a companion JSON properties file for each template.
explanationIncorrect: There is no required-workflows directory convention for starter templates; required workflows are configured through rulesets, not file placement. Starter workflows are not associated with a branch on the target repository. The organization wiki stores documentation and cannot surface runnable workflow templates on the Actions tab.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: A team attaches self-hosted runners to a public repository. A contributor forks the repository and opens a pull request with a modified workflow. Why is this a security concern even if fork PR approval is required?

options.text: The self-hosted runner cannot process pull_request events from forks at all
GitHub-hosted runners are always used for fork pull requests regardless of runs-on
The fork's GITHUB_TOKEN gains write access to the upstream repository automatically
Once a maintainer approves the run, the attacker's code executes on the team's self-hosted runner and network

explanationCorrect: Even with fork PR approval enabled, the maintainer must decide whether to approve each run. Once approved, the workflow executes on the self-hosted runner, giving the attacker's modified code access to the runner's host, network, and any credentials available on the machine. The approval step reduces the risk but does not eliminate it if the reviewer does not carefully inspect the workflow changes.
explanationIncorrect: Self-hosted runners can process pull_request events from forks; there is no such restriction, so the claim that they cannot is wrong. A fork PR's GITHUB_TOKEN has limited permissions scoped to the fork, not automatic write access to the upstream repository, so the claim about write access is also incorrect. GitHub does not override runs-on to force GitHub-hosted runners for fork PRs; the job runs on whatever runner the workflow specifies. The real danger is that once a maintainer approves the run, the forked workflow executes on the self-hosted runner where it can access the host network, environment variables, cached credentials, and any tools or secrets available on that machine.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: Twenty repositories need the same DEPLOY_TOKEN secret. The admin wants to rotate it in one place. Which feature avoids duplicating the secret in each repository?

options.text: An environment-level secret on each repository's production environment
A repository variable (not secret) set in each repository's settings
An organization secret scoped to the selected repositories that need it
A workflow-level env: block that hardcodes the token value in each workflow file

explanationCorrect: Organization-level secrets are defined once and shared with selected repositories through an access policy. Rotating the value in one place immediately takes effect for all repositories that reference it.
explanationIncorrect: Environment-level secrets are scoped per repository per environment, so you would still need to configure and rotate the value in each of the twenty repositories. A repository variable is unencrypted and visible in logs, making it unsuitable for tokens or credentials. Hardcoding a token in a workflow env: block commits the secret to the repository source, which is a serious security violation.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: The finance team asks which repositories are consuming the most Actions minutes. Where can an organization admin find a per-repository breakdown of minute usage?

options.text: The Security overview tab, which lists workflow consumption alongside vulnerabilities
The Insights traffic graph on each repository's Code tab
The Dependency graph, which includes compute costs alongside dependency data
The organization billing settings, which provide Actions usage reports downloadable as CSV

explanationCorrect: The organization billing and usage settings expose Actions minute consumption with per-repository detail. Admins can also download usage reports as CSV files for analysis and chargeback.
explanationIncorrect: The Security overview aggregates code scanning, secret scanning, and Dependabot alerts; it does not track compute minute consumption. The Insights traffic graph reports page views and git clones, not Actions usage. The Dependency graph maps software dependencies and has no connection to billed compute minutes.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An organization sets default GITHUB_TOKEN permissions to read-only. A repository admin then sets the repository's default to read-write in its own Actions settings. A workflow in that repository has no permissions block. What scope does the token receive?

options.text: Read-write, because the repository-level setting overrides the organization default
Read-only, because the organization default always takes precedence over repository settings
The workflow fails because the conflicting settings create an invalid configuration
No permissions at all, because conflicting defaults cancel each other out

explanationCorrect: The organization default applies when neither the repository nor the workflow overrides it. When a repository admin explicitly sets the default to read-write in that repository's Actions settings, the repository-level setting takes effect for workflows without a permissions block.
explanationIncorrect: The organization setting is a default for repositories that have not chosen their own setting, not an immutable ceiling. When the repository explicitly overrides it, the repository's choice prevails. Conflicting defaults do not cause a workflow failure; GitHub resolves the effective permission through the override chain. Permissions never cancel to zero; one level's setting always determines the effective default.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: A runner group exists at the organization level. An admin wants to make the runners in this group available only to private repositories, excluding public ones. Where is this restriction applied?

options.text: In each workflow's runs-on field by adding a private-only label
In the organization's Dependabot settings, which gate runner visibility
In each repository's branch protection settings under runner access
In the runner group settings, which allow restricting access to selected repositories

explanationCorrect: Runner group settings include a repository access policy where you select exactly which repositories may use the group's runners. The admin can include only the private repositories, excluding the public ones.
explanationIncorrect: Labels route jobs to runners but do not enforce access restrictions; any repository can target any label. Branch protection settings govern merging rules and do not include runner access controls. Dependabot settings manage dependency update configuration and have no connection to runner group visibility.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: A workflow deploying to GCP currently reads a service-account JSON key from a repository secret. The security team wants to eliminate this standing credential. What should replace it?

options.text: Move the JSON key to an organization secret so it is centrally managed
Encode the JSON key as base64 in a repository variable instead of a secret
Configure OIDC federation with GCP Workload Identity so the workflow receives short-lived tokens
Store the JSON key in a GitHub environment with a wait timer to limit access windows

explanationCorrect: OIDC federation with GCP Workload Identity lets the workflow present GitHub's OIDC token and receive short-lived credentials from GCP, eliminating the need to store any long-lived service account key.
explanationIncorrect: Moving the key to an organization secret centralizes management but the credential is still a long-lived JSON key that could be compromised. Encoding the key as base64 in a repository variable actually makes it worse: variables are not encrypted and appear in logs. An environment wait timer delays job execution but does nothing to replace the standing credential; the same long-lived key is still stored and used.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An enterprise configures a required workflow via an organization ruleset targeting all repositories. A repository owner deletes all workflow files from their repository. Does the required workflow still run on their pull requests?

options.text: No, required workflows need at least one local workflow file to trigger
No, deleting workflow files disables Actions entirely for that repository
Yes, the ruleset enforces the workflow independently of the repository's own files
Yes, but only if the repository still has a .github directory with at least one YAML file inside

explanationCorrect: Required workflows configured via organization rulesets are enforced independently of the repository's own workflow files. Even if a repository has no workflows of its own, the required workflow still runs on pull requests because the trigger comes from the ruleset, not from local files.
explanationIncorrect: Required workflows do not depend on the existence of local workflow files. Deleting workflow files does not disable Actions for the repository; Actions remains enabled as long as the org or repo settings allow it. The presence or absence of a .github directory is irrelevant; the ruleset enforcement is at the organization level and does not check for that directory.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An organization mirrors a specific SHA of actions/checkout into an internal repository and references the internal copy in all workflows. What is the primary security benefit?

options.text: The internal copy runs faster because it avoids downloading from the public repository each time
The internal copy automatically receives upstream security patches without manual intervention
The internal copy allows the workflow to skip the actions/checkout step entirely
The organization controls exactly which version runs, insulating workflows from upstream supply-chain attacks

explanationCorrect: Mirroring a vetted SHA into an internal repository means the organization decides when to update. If the upstream action is compromised or its tag is repointed, the internal workflows are unaffected because they reference the internal copy, not the public one.
explanationIncorrect: Performance is a minor side effect at best; the primary motivation is supply-chain security, not speed. An internal mirror does not automatically receive upstream patches; updates must be manually pulled and reviewed, which is the whole point of the control. Mirroring the action does not eliminate the need for the checkout step; the mirrored copy still performs the same checkout operation.

stem: A team's CI workflow needs to invoke a shared build workflow stored in .github/workflows/build.yml of a central repository. At what level is the call made?

options.text: At the step level with - uses: org/central/.github/workflows/build.yml@main
At the job level, with needs: pointing at the external workflow file path
At the job level, with jobs.<id>.uses: org/central/.github/workflows/build.yml@main
At the workflow level, with on: workflow_run referencing the central workflow

explanationCorrect: A reusable workflow is invoked at the job level with jobs.<id>.uses: pointing at the workflow file and a ref. The calling job becomes a thin wrapper whose entire execution is the called workflow's jobs.
explanationIncorrect: Steps call actions, not entire workflows — putting a workflow path under steps.uses would fail because the runner expects an action, not a workflow. needs orders jobs within the same workflow and does not accept external file paths. workflow_run triggers a workflow after another in the same repo completes; it does not compose an external workflow into the current run.

stem: What trigger must a workflow file declare to be callable as a reusable workflow by other workflows?

options.text: on: workflow_dispatch, which allows both manual and programmatic invocation
on: workflow_run, which fires when another workflow triggers it
on: repository_dispatch with a custom event type matching the caller
on: workflow_call, which defines the inputs, secrets, and outputs contract

explanationCorrect: A workflow becomes reusable by triggering on workflow_call, which also lets it declare inputs, secrets, and outputs for its callers. Without this trigger, the workflow cannot be composed into another.
explanationIncorrect: workflow_dispatch enables a manual Run button in the UI and API-based triggering, but it does not establish the caller-callee contract needed for reusable workflows. workflow_run triggers after another workflow completes, but it creates a separate run rather than composing into the caller's run. repository_dispatch fires on API events with custom payloads but does not provide the typed inputs, secrets, or outputs interface that reusable workflows need.

stem: A caller job invokes a reusable workflow and must forward all of its own secrets without listing each one. Which syntax does this?

options.text: with: secrets: ${{ toJSON(secrets) }} to serialize all secrets as a JSON input
secrets: forward-all: true under the calling job's configuration
env: ${{ secrets }} at the job level to expose all secrets as environment variables
secrets: inherit on the calling job, which passes every available secret

explanationCorrect: secrets: inherit on the calling job passes all of the caller's accessible secrets to the reusable workflow without naming each one individually. The reusable workflow can then reference them as if they were its own.
explanationIncorrect: Serializing secrets with toJSON and passing them as an input would expose all secret values as a single unmasked string — this is dangerous and not the intended mechanism. Assigning ${{ secrets }} to env is not valid syntax and would not correctly forward secrets to a reusable workflow's secrets context. There is no forward-all key under secrets; the keyword to pass all secrets implicitly is simply inherit.

stem: A reusable workflow computes a deployment URL as an output. How does the caller workflow access it in a subsequent job?

options.text: Via steps.<reusable-step>.outputs.<name> in any job that follows
Via env.DEPLOYMENT_URL, which the reusable workflow injects automatically
Via needs.<calling-job-id>.outputs.<name> after listing it in needs
Reusable workflows cannot return outputs to their callers

explanationCorrect: A reusable workflow declares outputs under workflow_call, and the caller reads them through needs.<jobId>.outputs.<name> by depending on the calling job — the same syntax as any job-to-job output dependency.
explanationIncorrect: The reusable workflow runs as a job, not a step, so its outputs are in the needs context, not the steps context. Outputs are not injected as environment variables automatically — you must reference them explicitly. Reusable workflows absolutely can return outputs when they are declared under the workflow_call trigger.

stem: What is the key structural difference between consuming a marketplace action and calling a reusable workflow?

options.text: An action runs as a step inside a job; a reusable workflow replaces an entire job definition
An action can only run on GitHub-hosted runners; a reusable workflow can run on self-hosted
A reusable workflow is limited to read-only GITHUB_TOKEN; actions can request write
An action cannot accept inputs; only reusable workflows support the with: key for inputs

explanationCorrect: Actions are the smallest reusable unit, called as a step inside a job via steps[].uses. Reusable workflows bundle complete jobs and are invoked at the job level with jobs.<id>.uses, so they operate at different granularities.
explanationIncorrect: Both actions and reusable workflows can run on either GitHub-hosted or self-hosted runners — the runner type is not a differentiator. Reusable workflows inherit the caller's permissions context and are not limited to read-only tokens. Actions accept inputs through with: on the step, so claiming they cannot accept inputs is false.

stem: After auditing your workflows, the security team finds that one action is pinned to @v3, another to a branch name, and a third to a commit SHA. Which pinning carries the highest supply-chain risk?

options.text: The commit SHA pin, because SHA references bypass tag-based vulnerability scanning
The @v3 tag pin, because tags are mutable and can be silently repointed
The branch pin, because it tracks the branch tip and changes with every push
All three carry equal risk since they all resolve to a commit eventually

explanationCorrect: A branch pin tracks the tip of that branch and changes with every push, giving you the least control and the highest exposure to unreviewed code changes. It is the riskiest of the three.
explanationIncorrect: A commit SHA is immutable and carries the lowest risk — it cannot be silently changed. SHA references do not bypass scanning; Dependabot can still flag known vulnerabilities in SHA-pinned actions. The @v3 tag is mutable and carries moderate risk, but it changes less frequently than a branch tip. They do not carry equal risk — immutability is the key differentiator, and these three options have very different immutability properties.

stem: When calling a reusable workflow, which key on the calling job passes non-sensitive input values to the called workflow's declared inputs?

options.text: inputs: on the calling job, mirroring the called workflow's inputs block
env: on the calling job, which maps environment variables to declared inputs
secrets: on the calling job, since all values passed to reusable workflows use secrets
with: on the calling job, matching the input names defined in workflow_call

explanationCorrect: The calling job passes declared inputs to a reusable workflow through the with: map, matching the input names the workflow_call trigger defines. This is the same key used to pass inputs to actions.
explanationIncorrect: The called workflow declares its parameters under inputs: in its workflow_call block, but the caller supplies values with with:, not inputs:. env: sets environment variables visible inside the job but does not map to the called workflow's declared inputs contract. secrets: passes sensitive values to the called workflow's declared secrets, not its inputs — the two are separate namespaces.

stem: A workflow's first step runs a linter on the repository code, but it fails with 'file not found' errors. The step before the linter is actions/setup-node. What is most likely missing?

options.text: An actions/checkout step before the linter, since the runner workspace starts empty
A permissions: contents: read block, since the default token cannot read the repository
An actions/download-artifact step to retrieve the code from a prior workflow run
A git clone command in a run step, since actions/checkout only works for private repos

explanationCorrect: A fresh runner has no repository content in its workspace. actions/setup-node configures the Node runtime but does not clone code. actions/checkout must run first to make the source files available for the linter.
explanationIncorrect: The default GITHUB_TOKEN already has contents: read in most configurations, so a missing permission would produce an auth error, not a file-not-found error. download-artifact retrieves artifacts from previous runs or jobs, not the repository source code. actions/checkout works for both public and private repositories — it is not private-only — and is the standard way to get code onto the runner.

stem: Workflow A calls reusable workflow B, which calls reusable workflow C, which calls D, which calls E. What happens when the run is triggered?

options.text: All five levels execute successfully, since there is no nesting limit for reusable workflows
The call from D to E fails because the maximum nesting depth of four levels is exceeded
Only A and B execute; reusable workflows cannot call other reusable workflows at all
The entire run fails at trigger time because GitHub detects a circular dependency

explanationCorrect: GitHub allows reusable workflow calls up to four levels deep. A→B→C→D is four levels, so D→E would be the fifth and exceeds the limit, causing that call to fail.
explanationIncorrect: There is a documented nesting limit of four levels, so unlimited nesting is incorrect. Reusable workflows can call other reusable workflows — the limit is depth, not a blanket prohibition. The chain A→B→C→D→E is not circular (no workflow calls back to one already in the chain), so GitHub would not flag it as a circular dependency — it simply exceeds the depth limit.

stem: How do you lock a reusable workflow reference to a specific release so upstream changes cannot alter what runs?

options.text: Append a branch filter inside the caller's on.push trigger configuration
Append a tag or commit SHA after @ in the uses reference, e.g. @v2 or @<sha>
Set the called workflow's concurrency group to the desired version string
Add a needs: entry that names the version of the called workflow explicitly

explanationCorrect: The @ref portion of a reusable workflow reference selects a tag, branch, or commit SHA; pinning to a tag like @v2 or a commit SHA ensures upstream changes on other refs do not affect your run.
explanationIncorrect: A branch filter on the caller's push trigger controls when the caller runs, not which version of the called workflow is used. Concurrency groups serialise overlapping runs and have no version-locking semantics. needs orders jobs within a workflow and does not select a version for a called workflow.

stem: Build times are long because npm dependencies are re-downloaded on every run. Which action provides a content-keyed cache that persists across runs?

options.text: actions/upload-artifact with a retention-days value matching the lockfile hash
actions/checkout with persist-credentials: true to store node_modules
actions/cache with a key derived from a hash of the lockfile
actions/setup-node with a registry-url that caches by default across runs

explanationCorrect: actions/cache stores and restores directories keyed on a value you choose; hashing the lockfile means the cache is reused while dependencies are unchanged and refreshed when they change.
explanationIncorrect: upload-artifact persists run outputs for download but is not a content-keyed dependency cache and does not accept a hash-based key. actions/checkout clones the repository and persist-credentials controls the git token, not dependency caching. actions/setup-node configures the Node runtime and can enable a built-in cache, but it delegates to actions/cache internally and registry-url alone does not enable cross-run caching.

stem: Where do you discover community actions, compare versions, and copy ready-to-use workflow snippets?

options.text: The repository's Projects board, which catalogues available actions
The repository's Discussions tab, which indexes action metadata
The repository's Wiki tab, which lists all published action versions
The GitHub Marketplace, which lists actions with usage snippets and versions

explanationCorrect: The GitHub Marketplace is the curated directory where published actions are listed with descriptions, version history, and copy-paste usage snippets for easy integration.
explanationIncorrect: Projects boards track work items and planning, not action discovery. Discussions hosts community Q&A but does not index action metadata or provide usage snippets. The Wiki holds free-form documentation for a single repository and is not a catalogue of actions across the ecosystem.

stem: A reusable workflow marks a secret named DEPLOY_KEY as required under workflow_call. The caller neither passes DEPLOY_KEY nor uses secrets: inherit. What is the outcome?

options.text: The run fails because a required secret was not supplied to the called workflow
The caller's repository-level secret of the same name is forwarded automatically
The called workflow reads DEPLOY_KEY as an empty string and continues
The called workflow skips every step that references the secret but still succeeds

explanationCorrect: When a reusable workflow declares a secret as required, the caller must supply it explicitly or via secrets: inherit; omitting it causes the run to fail validation before any job starts.
explanationIncorrect: A required secret does not silently default to an empty string; that is the purpose of making it required. Caller secrets are not forwarded automatically without inherit or an explicit mapping. The workflow does not selectively skip steps; it fails outright when a required secret is missing.

stem: A step has continue-on-error: true and it fails. A later step checks steps.flaky.outcome and steps.flaky.conclusion. What values do those hold?

options.text: Both outcome and conclusion are 'success' because continue-on-error hides the failure
outcome is 'failure' (raw result); conclusion is 'success' (after continue-on-error)
outcome is 'success' (adjusted); conclusion is 'failure' (raw result)
Both are 'failure' — continue-on-error only affects the job status, not step fields

explanationCorrect: A step's outcome is its raw result before continue-on-error is applied, so it shows 'failure'. The conclusion reflects the result after continue-on-error turns the failure into 'success' for the purposes of the job continuing.
explanationIncorrect: Both being 'success' would mean there is no way to detect that the step actually failed, which defeats the purpose of having two distinct fields. The reversed version (outcome = success, conclusion = failure) has the semantics backward — outcome is always the raw, unadjusted result. Both being 'failure' would mean continue-on-error has no observable effect on step metadata, but it does — it adjusts the conclusion while preserving the raw outcome for inspection.

stem: A matrix build should keep running all legs even if one fails, and you also want at most three legs executing simultaneously. Which two strategy keys do you set?

options.text: continue-on-error: true and concurrency: 3 on the job
fail-fast: true and max-parallel: 3 under strategy
fail-fast: false and strategy.matrix.parallel: 3
fail-fast: false and max-parallel: 3 under strategy

explanationCorrect: fail-fast: false stops one failing combination from cancelling the rest, and max-parallel: 3 caps how many matrix jobs run concurrently. Both live under the strategy key.
explanationIncorrect: continue-on-error changes how a job's failure is reported to downstream jobs rather than the matrix cancellation behavior, and concurrency is a workflow/job-level key for run serialization, not a numeric matrix throttle. fail-fast: true is the default that cancels remaining jobs on the first failure — the opposite of what is wanted. matrix.parallel is not a real key; the concurrency throttle lives directly under strategy as max-parallel, not nested inside matrix. The correct pair is fail-fast: false and max-parallel: 3.

stem: Job build produces a compiled binary that job deploy needs. The two jobs run on separate runners. What is the standard way to pass the file between them?

options.text: Upload with actions/upload-artifact in build, download with actions/download-artifact in deploy
Use actions/cache keyed on the job name to store and restore the binary
Pass the binary as a job output string through the needs context
Write the binary path to $GITHUB_ENV so deploy inherits the variable

explanationCorrect: Artifacts are the intended mechanism for moving files between jobs: build uploads the binary as an artifact and deploy downloads it, which works even though each job runs on a separate runner.
explanationIncorrect: actions/cache is designed for speeding up repeated dependency restores keyed by a content hash, not for reliably handing a specific build output to a downstream job — cache eviction could cause deploy to miss the file. Job outputs are strings passed through the needs context with limited size; they cannot carry a binary file. $GITHUB_ENV only sets environment variables within the same job and does not cross the job boundary to a different runner. The correct tool for passing files between jobs is upload-artifact and download-artifact.

stem: A workflow_dispatch trigger defines a choice input named environment with options staging and production. How does a step read the user's selection?

options.text: ${{ vars.environment }} from the repository variables context
${{ inputs.environment }} or ${{ github.event.inputs.environment }}
${{ secrets.environment }} since dispatch inputs are treated as secrets
${{ matrix.environment }} expanded from the dispatch as a matrix axis

explanationCorrect: Manual dispatch inputs are available through the inputs context and, for backward compatibility, through github.event.inputs. Both paths return the selected value.
explanationIncorrect: The vars context holds repository or organization configuration variables set in Settings, not dispatch inputs — they are separate concepts. The secrets context exposes configured secrets and dispatch inputs are not stored as secrets. Dispatch inputs do not automatically become matrix axes — a matrix must be explicitly declared under strategy and has nothing to do with workflow_dispatch inputs. The correct context for dispatch inputs is inputs (or github.event.inputs).

stem: A job needs to read repository code and write check-run results, nothing more. Following least privilege, which permissions block is correct?

options.text: permissions: read-all — grants read on every scope including checks
permissions: {} — then add checks: write in a step-level override
permissions: { contents: read, checks: write }
permissions: write-all — covers all write needs including checks

explanationCorrect: Declaring only contents: read and checks: write grants exactly the scopes the job needs and implicitly drops all others to none, matching least privilege.
explanationIncorrect: read-all grants read on every scope (issues, packages, actions, deployments, etc.), which is broader than needed and does not grant the checks: write the job requires. An empty permissions map sets every scope to none, and there is no step-level permissions override — permissions can only be set at the workflow or job level, so the step override described does not exist. write-all grants write across all scopes, which is the opposite of least privilege. The narrow declaration is contents: read plus checks: write.

stem: Which uses reference correctly calls a reusable workflow stored in another repository at a pinned release?

options.text: uses: octo-org/shared/build.yml@v2 (path without .github/workflows)
uses: octo-org/shared/.github/workflows/build.yml@v2
uses: ./.github/workflows/build.yml@v2 (relative path with ref)
run: gh workflow run octo-org/shared/.github/workflows/build.yml@v2

explanationCorrect: A cross-repository reusable workflow is referenced as owner/repo/.github/workflows/file.yml@ref, including the full path under .github/workflows and a branch, tag, or SHA.
explanationIncorrect: Dropping the .github/workflows/ segment makes the reference invalid because reusable workflows must reside in that directory and be addressed through it. The ./ relative form works only within the same repository and does not accept an @ref suffix. Using run with gh workflow run triggers a separate workflow_dispatch call rather than composing the workflow inline.

stem: A caller wants the reusable workflow it invokes to receive every secret the caller has, without listing each one individually. What syntax achieves this?

options.text: secrets: inherit on the calling job
permissions: secrets: read on the calling job
with: secrets: ${{ toJSON(secrets) }} on the calling job
env: SECRETS: ${{ secrets }} on the calling job

explanationCorrect: secrets: inherit on the calling job passes every secret available to the caller down to the reusable workflow without naming them individually.
explanationIncorrect: permissions controls GITHUB_TOKEN scopes and has no secrets: read option that forwards repository secrets. Serializing secrets with toJSON under with would treat them as a regular input string, not as the secrets context the called workflow expects. Mapping secrets to an env variable exposes them as a single environment variable rather than populating the called workflow's secrets context.

stem: A reusable workflow declares outputs under workflow_call.outputs that map from a job's outputs. In the calling workflow, a downstream job needs one of those values. Which expression reads it?

options.text: steps.<callJobId>.outputs.<outputName> in the downstream job
jobs.<callJobId>.result.<outputName> in the downstream job
env.<outputName> automatically injected into the downstream job
needs.<callJobId>.outputs.<outputName> in the downstream job

explanationCorrect: The reusable workflow's declared outputs surface on the calling job, so a downstream job with a needs dependency reads them via needs.<callJobId>.outputs.<outputName>.
explanationIncorrect: The steps context holds outputs from steps within the current job, not from another job that called a reusable workflow. There is no jobs.<id>.result expression for reading cross-job outputs at runtime. The outputs are not automatically injected as environment variables; they must be read explicitly through the needs context.

stem: Which reference style for a third-party Marketplace action is truly immutable, preventing a moved tag from silently changing the code that runs?

options.text: A major version tag like actions/checkout@v4, since tags cannot be repointed
A branch name like actions/checkout@main for the latest stable code
A full commit SHA like actions/checkout@8f4b7f84... reviewed before pinning
A semver range like actions/checkout@^4.0.0 to lock to compatible releases

explanationCorrect: A full commit SHA is immutable; even if a maintainer's tag is moved or their account is compromised, your workflow runs the exact code at that SHA until you deliberately update it.
explanationIncorrect: Git tags are mutable references a maintainer can repoint at any time, so a major version tag is not immutable. A branch like main advances with every merge and offers no reproducibility. GitHub Actions does not support semver ranges in uses references, so that syntax is invalid.

stem: A composite action declares two inputs: region and stage. When consuming it in a workflow step, how do you supply those values?

options.text: List them under a secrets: block on the step alongside uses
Provide them in a with: block on the step alongside uses
Set them in the job-level strategy.matrix and reference matrix values
Export them as shell variables in a prior run: step for automatic binding

explanationCorrect: Action inputs are supplied through the with map on the step that references the action, mapping each key to the action's declared input names.
explanationIncorrect: The secrets block on a job passes secrets to reusable workflows, not inputs to action steps. A matrix fans out job combinations and does not bind action inputs directly. Shell variables exported in a prior step do not populate the action's inputs context; only with provides that binding.

stem: You want a step to run a container image from a public registry directly, without a separate action repository. Which uses syntax is valid?

options.text: uses: docker://alpine:3.19 with the docker:// scheme
uses: container://alpine:3.19 with the container:// scheme
uses: alpine:3.19 as a bare image reference without a scheme
uses: oci://alpine:3.19 with the oci:// scheme for OCI images

explanationCorrect: A step can run a published container image directly with uses: docker://<image>:<tag>, which tells the runner to pull and execute the image as a container action.
explanationIncorrect: There is no container:// scheme recognised by the uses keyword. A bare image reference without a scheme is ambiguous and not valid syntax for uses. The oci:// scheme is not supported by GitHub Actions, so docker:// is the correct and only recognised image scheme.

stem: A reusable workflow declares a numeric input build_number under workflow_call.inputs. How does the caller supply its value?

options.text: Under the calling job's env: block, mapping build_number to a value
Under the calling job's secrets: block, naming build_number explicitly
Under the calling job's with: block, e.g. with: { build_number: 42 }
Under the calling job's needs: block, referencing a prior job output

explanationCorrect: Inputs declared under workflow_call are passed by the caller through the with map on the job that uses the reusable workflow, matching key names to the declared inputs.
explanationIncorrect: An env block sets environment variables for the job's own steps but does not bind to a called workflow's declared inputs. The secrets block passes secrets, which are a separate channel from inputs. needs establishes job ordering and lets you read outputs, but it does not supply inputs to a called workflow.

stem: A caller in one repository passes secrets: inherit to a reusable workflow in a different repository within the same organization. The call fails. What is the most likely missing prerequisite?

options.text: The calling job lacks permissions: id-token: write for cross-repo authentication
The reusable workflow's repository has not granted Actions access to the caller
secrets: inherit only works within the same repository, never cross-repo
The caller must also declare on: workflow_call in its own workflow file

explanationCorrect: Cross-repository reuse requires the reusable workflow's repository to explicitly grant Actions access to the calling repository (or the whole organization) in its settings; without that, the call is rejected.
explanationIncorrect: id-token: write controls OIDC token generation, not cross-repo workflow access. secrets: inherit does work cross-repo once access is granted, so the claim it never works is false. The caller does not need workflow_call in its own file; workflow_call is declared only by the callee to indicate it is reusable.

stem: A JavaScript action needs a file at its root that declares runs.using, the entry point, and the action's input/output contract. What is that file?

options.text: Dockerfile, which defines both the runtime environment and entry point
package.json, where the main field doubles as the action entry point
action.yml (or action.yaml), which declares runs.using and the input/output contract
index.js itself, which self-registers its inputs and outputs at runtime

explanationCorrect: Every action is defined by an action.yml (or action.yaml) metadata file that declares inputs, outputs, and the runs configuration including using and main.
explanationIncorrect: A Dockerfile is only needed for Docker container actions and still must be referenced from action.yml; it does not replace the metadata file. package.json describes an npm package but is not the action metadata file the runner reads for inputs, outputs, and runs.using. A JavaScript entry file runs after the runner reads action.yml; it cannot self-register metadata before the runner knows how to execute it.

stem: Why is committing a bundled file produced by ncc preferred over committing the raw node_modules directory for a JavaScript action?

options.text: Bundling transpiles TypeScript, which is the only language the runner supports
Bundling encrypts the source code so that consumers cannot inspect it
node_modules works identically but bundling reduces checkout size and avoids thousands of files
Bundling is mandatory to list the action on the GitHub Marketplace

explanationCorrect: Both approaches work because the runner does not run npm install, but bundling into a single file dramatically reduces the number of committed files and checkout size, making the repository cleaner and faster to clone.
explanationIncorrect: Bundling does not encrypt or hide source; the output is still readable JavaScript. The runner executes JavaScript, not TypeScript directly, but transpilation is a separate concern from why bundling beats committing node_modules. Bundling is not a Marketplace requirement; it is a practical choice for repository hygiene and performance.

stem: Which action.yml keys let a JavaScript action run setup logic before the main step and cleanup logic after the job's other steps complete?

options.text: steps.before and steps.after within the runs block
runs.pre and runs.post, each pointing to a separate script file
hooks.setup and hooks.teardown under the action's branding section
jobs.pre and jobs.post defined alongside the runs.main entry

explanationCorrect: A JavaScript action can declare runs.pre and runs.post scripts that execute before and after the main entry point, useful for setup and cleanup.
explanationIncorrect: There are no steps.before or steps.after keys in action metadata; steps are a composite action concept. hooks.setup and hooks.teardown are not part of the action.yml schema, and branding only configures Marketplace icons and colors. jobs.pre and jobs.post are not action metadata keys; jobs belong to workflows, not actions.

stem: Where in action.yml do you configure the icon and color shown on the GitHub Marketplace listing for your action?

options.text: Under the branding key with icon and color sub-fields
In a separate marketplace.json file alongside action.yml
In the repository's README.md front matter with YAML headers
In the calling workflow's with: block when referencing the action

explanationCorrect: The branding section of action.yml lets you set an icon and color used on the action's Marketplace listing, choosing from Feather icons and preset colors.
explanationIncorrect: There is no marketplace.json convention for configuring branding; it lives in action.yml. A README has no front matter that controls Marketplace branding; it only provides the listing description. A consuming workflow cannot set the branding of an action it merely calls; branding is metadata owned by the action author.

stem: An action input should be optional with a fallback value. How do you express that in action.yml?

options.text: Set required: true and provide a default, forcing callers to confirm the value
Place the input under outputs: with a default field to make it bidirectional
Provide the fallback only in the consuming workflow's env: block, not in action.yml
Set required: false and provide a default under the input declaration

explanationCorrect: Marking an input required: false with a default lets callers omit it while the action still receives the fallback value.
explanationIncorrect: Marking required: true signals callers must supply the input, contradicting optional behavior even if a default exists. Inputs belong under inputs:, not outputs:, and there is no bidirectional concept. Defining the fallback only in the workflow's env: block means other callers would not get the fallback, and it does not populate the inputs context.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An enterprise's Actions policy allows only select actions. A developer adds a uses: reference to a new third-party action not on the allow list. What happens when the workflow runs?

options.text: The job fails because the action is not permitted by the organization's Actions policy
The workflow runs normally but the action's outputs are redacted for security
The workflow queues indefinitely until an admin adds the action to the allow list
The action runs in a sandboxed mode with no access to secrets or the repository

explanationCorrect: When the Actions policy restricts usage to an allow list, any reference to an action not on the list causes the job to fail with an error indicating the action is not allowed.
explanationIncorrect: There is no output-redaction mode for disallowed actions; the action simply cannot execute. The workflow does not queue indefinitely waiting for approval; it fails immediately. GitHub Actions has no sandboxed execution mode for policy-blocked actions; the policy is binary — allowed or rejected.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: Runners in a group labelled deploy-prod can reach production. The team adds a new runner to this group but workflows still report 'no matching runner found.' What should they check first?

options.text: Whether the new runner has the same custom labels that workflows specify in runs-on
Whether the repository's branch protection requires the deploy-prod status check
Whether the workflow's concurrency group matches the runner group name
Whether the runner has permissions: id-token: write in its registration

explanationCorrect: Being in the correct runner group grants access, but the runner also needs the specific custom labels that workflows reference in runs-on. If the new runner is missing a label like deploy-prod, it will not match even though it is in the right group.
explanationIncorrect: Branch protection status checks gate merging and have nothing to do with runner matching. Concurrency groups control run serialization and are unrelated to runner group names or runner discovery. The permissions: id-token: write setting is a workflow-level token permission, not a runner registration property.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: A security audit finds that a self-hosted runner used for a public repository had a prior job's credentials still in /tmp. Which runner configuration would have prevented this?

options.text: Adding more labels to the runner so fewer jobs are routed to it
Configuring the runner as ephemeral so it handles one job then is destroyed
Moving the runner to a concurrency group with cancel-in-progress: true
Setting permissions: contents: read on all workflows that use the runner

explanationCorrect: Ephemeral runners are torn down after completing a single job. Since the runner is destroyed, no files or credentials from a prior job can persist for the next one to find.
explanationIncorrect: Adding labels changes routing but does not clean the runner between jobs; leftover files remain regardless of how many labels exist. Concurrency groups and cancel-in-progress control run overlap, not workspace hygiene between sequential jobs. Scoping the GITHUB_TOKEN to read-only limits API access but does not prevent a job from writing files to /tmp that persist for the next job on a non-ephemeral runner.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An incident responder needs to determine which user changed the organization's Actions permissions policy last Tuesday. Which data source contains this information?

options.text: The workflow run log for the most recent Actions run in the repository
The repository's git log showing commits to .github/workflows
The organization audit log filtered for Actions policy change events
The Dependabot alerts timeline for the organization

explanationCorrect: The organization (or enterprise) audit log records administrative events including changes to Actions permissions policies, with timestamps and the actor who made the change. Filtering by event type and date surfaces the specific change.
explanationIncorrect: Workflow run logs show the output of a specific run's steps and do not record administrative settings changes. The git log tracks commits to files in the repository; Actions policy changes are made through the UI or API and are not committed to any repository. Dependabot alerts track vulnerable dependencies and have no connection to Actions settings.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: Private repository workflows are consuming more Actions minutes than budgeted. The admin wants to cap overage spending. Which setting provides this control?

options.text: A spending limit for GitHub Actions configured in the organization's billing settings
A timeout-minutes value on every workflow file across all repositories
A concurrency setting on each workflow to limit parallel runs
A matrix max-parallel value that reduces how many jobs run simultaneously

explanationCorrect: The billing settings allow organizations to set a spending limit for Actions that caps how much overage beyond the included minutes can be charged, providing a hard budget boundary.
explanationIncorrect: timeout-minutes limits individual job duration but does not cap total monthly spending across all workflows and repositories. Concurrency limits restrict how many runs of the same workflow overlap but do not bound total billed minutes. Matrix max-parallel reduces parallelism within a single run, which may extend wall-clock time but does not reduce total minutes consumed or control billing.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: Actions Runner Controller (ARC) is deployed on Kubernetes with a runner scale set configured for minimum replicas of 0. Jobs occasionally take several minutes to start. What explains the delay?

options.text: The runner group's repository access policy is blocking the workflow
The OIDC token is taking time to be issued by GitHub before the runner can authenticate
The workflow's concurrency group is holding the run in a queue behind another run
When scaled to zero, ARC must provision a new pod and register a runner before the job can be picked up

explanationCorrect: With minimum replicas set to zero, there are no idle runners waiting. When a job is queued, ARC detects the demand and provisions a new Kubernetes pod, which must start, register with GitHub, and become idle before it can pick up the job. This cold-start sequence explains the multi-minute delay.
explanationIncorrect: A runner group access policy block would cause the job to fail with no matching runner, not a delay followed by eventual execution. OIDC token issuance occurs during the job's steps, not during runner provisioning, so it does not explain a delay before the job starts. A concurrency group would be visible in the workflow run UI as 'waiting' with a clear reason, and is unrelated to runner provisioning time.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An organization's .github repository has a workflow-templates directory containing ci.yml and ci.properties.json. What does the properties file control?

options.text: It defines the template's display name, description, icon, and which repository file patterns it applies to
It stores encrypted secrets that the template workflow uses at runtime
It specifies which runners the template should target via a runs-on override
It pins the versions of all actions referenced by the template workflow

explanationCorrect: The properties JSON file provides metadata for the starter workflow template: its display name, description, Octicon icon, and optional filePatterns that control which repositories see the template suggestion based on the languages or files they contain.
explanationIncorrect: The properties file is metadata for the Actions tab UI; it does not store secrets, which must be configured in repository or organization settings. It does not override runs-on; the workflow YAML itself specifies the runner. It does not pin action versions; version pinning is done within the workflow file's uses: references.

stem: A workflow should trigger only on pull requests that target the main branch. Which trigger configuration expresses this?

options.text: on: pull_request with a paths filter of ['main/**']
on: push with a branches filter of ['main']
on: pull_request with a tags filter of ['main']
on: pull_request with a branches filter of ['main']

explanationCorrect: The pull_request event accepts a branches filter that scopes runs to PRs whose base (target) branch matches, so branches: ['main'] fires only for PRs targeting main.
explanationIncorrect: A paths filter limits triggers based on which files changed, not which branch the PR targets — paths: ['main/**'] would look for changed files in a directory called main, not the main branch. The push event fires on direct pushes, not pull requests, so it cannot filter PR targets. Pull requests do not have tags — the tags filter exists on push events for git tag pushes and is not available on pull_request. The correct mechanism is pull_request with a branches filter.

stem: A release job should start only after both the build job and the test job finish successfully. How do you express this fan-in dependency?

options.text: Set if: always() on the release job so it waits for everything
Set needs: [build, test] on the release job
Set continue-on-error: true on both build and test
Place release below build and test in the YAML file for ordering

explanationCorrect: The needs key accepts an array of job ids; the dependent job waits until all listed jobs complete successfully before it starts, creating the fan-in.
explanationIncorrect: always() forces a job to run regardless of upstream results, which is the opposite of gating on success — it would run release even if build or test failed. continue-on-error lets a job fail without failing the run but establishes no ordering and would allow release to run before or alongside the other jobs. YAML key order in the jobs map has no effect on execution — jobs run in parallel by default unless ordered by needs. The fan-in dependency is needs: [build, test].

stem: A deploy step should run only when all previous steps succeeded AND the branch is main. Which if expression combines both conditions correctly?

options.text: failure() || github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
always() && github.ref_name == 'refs/heads/main'
success() && github.ref == 'main'
success() && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'

explanationCorrect: success() is true when all prior steps passed, and github.ref for a branch push is the full ref refs/heads/main. Combining them with && gates the step on both conditions.
explanationIncorrect: failure() || would run the step when things fail or when on main, which is wrong — it would deploy after failures. always() ignores prior failures and would allow the deploy step to run even if earlier steps failed, which is dangerous for a deploy. Comparing github.ref to the bare string 'main' fails because github.ref is always the full ref path refs/heads/main, not the short name. The correct expression is success() && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'.

stem: The same test steps must run once for each of three Node.js versions in parallel. Which construct is designed for this fan-out?

options.text: A build matrix under strategy.matrix listing the three versions
Three separate needs chains running sequentially
A concurrency group with three slots
Three workflow_dispatch inputs, one per version to test

explanationCorrect: strategy.matrix expands a single job definition into one run per listed value, so listing three Node versions produces three parallel jobs from one definition.
explanationIncorrect: Three separate needs chains create sequential dependencies, not parallel fan-out from a single definition, and require duplicating the job definition. Concurrency groups serialize runs and have no concept of 'slots' for parallelism — they control how overlapping runs queue, not how a job fans out. workflow_dispatch inputs are user-provided values for manual triggers, not a mechanism for automated parallel expansion across versions. The construct for parameterized fan-out is strategy.matrix.

stem: Pushes that only change files under docs/ should not trigger the CI workflow. Which trigger filter prevents this?

options.text: on: push with branches-ignore: ['docs/**'] to exclude the docs branch
A job-level if: github.event.head_commit.modified != 'docs/' condition
on: push with paths-ignore: ['docs/**'] to skip docs-only changes
on: push with paths: ['!docs/**'] using negation in the inclusion list

explanationCorrect: paths-ignore skips the workflow when every changed file in the push matches the given path globs, so 'docs/**' avoids runs for docs-only changes while still triggering for any other file.
explanationIncorrect: branches-ignore filters by branch name, not by which files changed — a docs glob there would match a branch literally named docs/something, not the docs directory in the repo. Checking head_commit.modified against a string does not work because modified is an array of filenames, not a single string, and a job-level if still consumes a workflow run rather than preventing the trigger. Negation with ! inside the paths list is not valid syntax — paths is an inclusion filter and paths-ignore is the dedicated exclusion mechanism. The correct filter is paths-ignore.

stem: A job must run on the latest Ubuntu image provided by GitHub-hosted runners. Which runs-on value is correct?

options.text: runs-on: self-hosted with a Linux label for Ubuntu
runs-on: ubuntu-22.04 to pin to the latest LTS release
container: ubuntu:latest under the job, with no runs-on
runs-on: ubuntu-latest

explanationCorrect: GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runners are selected with the label ubuntu-latest, which always maps to the current latest supported Ubuntu image maintained by GitHub.
explanationIncorrect: self-hosted with a Linux label selects a self-hosted runner, not a GitHub-hosted one — you must operate that infrastructure yourself. ubuntu-22.04 pins to a specific version, which may not be the latest as GitHub rolls forward (e.g., ubuntu-24.04 may already be available). A container: block runs the job's steps inside a Docker container on top of whatever runner is assigned — it still requires a runs-on value, and using a bare ubuntu:latest Docker image lacks the preinstalled tools that GitHub-hosted runner images provide. The correct label is ubuntu-latest.

stem: An organization's GITHUB_TOKEN default is read-write. A security-conscious workflow author wants a job's token scoped to only read repository contents. Which declaration achieves this at the job level?

options.text: A permissions block on the job with contents: read and no other scopes listed
An env block setting GITHUB_TOKEN to a read-only personal access token
A permissions block on the job with read-all to cover contents read access
A secrets block referencing GITHUB_TOKEN with a read-only modifier

explanationCorrect: A job-level permissions block listing only contents: read grants that scope and implicitly drops all others to none, overriding the organization's broader default with a least-privilege declaration.
explanationIncorrect: Overriding GITHUB_TOKEN via env with a personal access token reintroduces long-lived credentials and does not actually change the automatic token's scopes. read-all grants read on every scope (issues, packages, actions, deployments, etc.), which is broader than 'only read repository contents' even though no write access is granted. There is no secrets block with a read-only modifier — secrets store values and have no access-level modifiers. The correct approach is an explicit permissions block with only the needed scope.

stem: What must a reusable workflow declare so that a calling workflow can pass a value into it?

options.text: A top-level env map with defaults for each expected value from callers
An on.push.inputs block listing each parameter name and its type
An on.workflow_call.inputs block listing each parameter name and its type
A jobs.<id>.strategy.matrix entry for each expected caller value

explanationCorrect: A callable workflow declares the parameters it accepts under on.workflow_call.inputs, each with a name and type, and reads them via the inputs context at runtime.
explanationIncorrect: A top-level env sets environment variables but does not define a caller-supplied input contract that validates types. The push event does not support an inputs declaration for callers; only workflow_call and workflow_dispatch support inputs. A matrix expands a job across value combinations but is not the mechanism for accepting caller-supplied parameters.

stem: A reusable workflow computes a deployment URL and must return it to the caller so a downstream job can use it. What does the reusable workflow define to expose that value?

options.text: An artifact uploaded with actions/upload-artifact that the caller downloads
on.workflow_call.outputs mapped from a job's outputs inside the workflow
A repository variable set dynamically via the GitHub API during the run
A step that appends the URL to $GITHUB_ENV, which the caller inherits

explanationCorrect: A reusable workflow declares on.workflow_call.outputs, mapping each output to a job output within the workflow, so the caller can read the returned value through the needs context.
explanationIncorrect: An artifact transfers files, not a structured output the caller reads through the needs context; it also requires separate download logic. Setting a repository variable via the API is persistent and visible to all runs, which is inappropriate for a per-run computed value. $GITHUB_ENV only carries environment variables within the same job; it does not cross the boundary back to the calling workflow.

stem: A team pins third-party actions to full commit SHAs instead of version tags. What is the primary security benefit of this practice?

options.text: SHA-pinned actions bypass the permissions block, reducing config overhead
SHA-pinned actions run faster because the runner caches them by hash
SHA-pinned actions automatically receive security patches from the maintainer
A SHA is immutable, so a compromised or repointed tag cannot change what runs

explanationCorrect: A commit SHA is immutable; pinning to it ensures the exact code you reviewed executes, even if the maintainer or an attacker later re-points a tag to different code.
explanationIncorrect: SHA pinning has no effect on the permissions block or GITHUB_TOKEN scopes. The runner does not cache actions differently based on whether the ref is a SHA or a tag. SHA pinning is the opposite of auto-updating; the action stays fixed until you manually update the SHA, so it does not receive patches automatically.

stem: Several workflows in the same repository repeat an identical five-step linting sequence. You want to extract it without creating a separate reusable workflow file. Which mechanism fits?

options.text: A composite action stored in the repository, referenced with uses: ./path
A concurrency group that runs the five steps in a shared queue
A matrix that expands the five steps into parallel jobs automatically
A YAML anchor defined once and referenced from each workflow file

explanationCorrect: A composite action packages multiple steps into one reusable action that any workflow in the same repository can call with uses: ./path-to-action, centralising the step sequence.
explanationIncorrect: A concurrency group serialises overlapping runs but does not encapsulate or reuse steps. A matrix fans a single job across value combinations; it does not extract and share a step sequence. GitHub Actions does not process YAML anchors across files, and even within a file the support is limited, so anchors cannot reliably share step definitions across workflows.

stem: A workflow omits actions/checkout entirely. What happens when the first run: step tries to access a source file?

options.text: The file is not found because the workspace is empty without a checkout step
The runner clones the repository automatically before every run: step
The runner downloads only the file that the run: step names on demand
The step reads from the previous workflow run's leftover workspace

explanationCorrect: GitHub-hosted runners start with an empty workspace; without actions/checkout the repository code is never fetched, so any step that tries to access a source file fails because the file does not exist.
explanationIncorrect: The runner does not automatically clone the repository; that is exactly what actions/checkout does explicitly. There is no on-demand file download mechanism for the workspace. GitHub-hosted runners are ephemeral and do not retain files from a previous workflow run.

stem: Which reference style follows the common convention for consuming a Marketplace action at a stable major version that still receives backward-compatible patches?

options.text: owner/action@v4 referencing the maintainer's moving major-version tag
owner/action@latest referencing the latest release tag automatically
owner/action@marketplace referencing the Marketplace publication ref
owner/action with no ref, which defaults to the latest major version

explanationCorrect: The common convention is to reference a Marketplace action with a major version tag like @v4, which maintainers move forward to the newest backward-compatible release so consumers get patches without breaking changes.
explanationIncorrect: @latest is not a standard convention and may not exist as a tag; most maintainers maintain major-version tags instead. @marketplace is not a git ref and does not exist as a tag or branch. Omitting the ref entirely is invalid syntax for a uses reference in GitHub Actions.

stem: A reusable workflow declares an input with type: string and a default value of 'production'. The caller does not supply that input. What value does the reusable workflow receive?

options.text: The string 'production', because the declared default fills in for the omission
An empty string, because callers must always provide every declared input
Null, because only required inputs receive defaults when omitted
The caller's repository name, used as a fallback when no value is given

explanationCorrect: When an input declares a default and the caller omits it, the reusable workflow uses that default value; in this case the input receives the string 'production'.
explanationIncorrect: The input does not become an empty string; the whole point of a default is to fill in when the caller omits the value. Null is not substituted; the default value is used regardless of whether the input is marked required. The caller's repository name is never used as an automatic fallback for omitted inputs.

stem: You publish a reusable workflow and want to restrict which repositories can call it. Where is this access boundary configured?

options.text: In the workflow file's on.workflow_call section with an allowed-repos list
In the repository's branch protection rules under required status checks
In the repository's Actions settings under access for reusable workflows
In the organization's runner group configuration for the repository

explanationCorrect: The repository's Actions settings include an access control that governs whether its workflows can be used by other repositories in the organization or enterprise, which is where you restrict callers.
explanationIncorrect: There is no allowed-repos list in the workflow_call trigger schema; access is managed in the repository settings, not the workflow file. Branch protection rules gate merging and status checks, not who may call a reusable workflow. Runner groups control which repositories can use specific runners, not which repositories can invoke reusable workflows.

stem: Workflow A calls reusable workflow B, which calls reusable workflow C. What constraint applies to this chain?

options.text: The nesting works only if all three workflows share the same repository
Each level of nesting doubles the required permissions on GITHUB_TOKEN
Reusable workflows cannot call other reusable workflows under any circumstance
GitHub enforces a maximum nesting depth, limiting how deep the chain can go

explanationCorrect: GitHub allows reusable workflows to call other reusable workflows but enforces a maximum nesting depth (currently four levels), preventing arbitrarily deep chains.
explanationIncorrect: Cross-repository nesting is supported as long as access is granted, so they do not need to share a repository. Nesting does not change GITHUB_TOKEN permissions; each workflow operates under its own permissions block. The claim that reusable workflows can never call others is incorrect; nesting has been supported since GitHub introduced the feature.

stem: In action.yml, which runs.using value declares a Docker container action?

options.text: composite, which runs steps inside a container automatically
docker, paired with an image: field referencing a Dockerfile or image
node20, with a container: override in the runs block
container, a dedicated value for Docker-based actions

explanationCorrect: A container action sets runs.using to docker and points image to a Dockerfile or published image that the runner builds and executes.
explanationIncorrect: composite indicates an action made of multiple steps that run on the host runner, not inside a container. node20 indicates a JavaScript action running on Node 20, and there is no container: override field in a JavaScript action's runs block. There is no 'container' value for runs.using; the valid values are docker, node20 (or other node versions), and composite.

stem: A JavaScript action must read the user-supplied input named repo and then set an output named status. Which @actions/core calls achieve both operations?

options.text: core.getInput('repo') to read, then core.exportVariable('status', val) to output
core.getInput('repo') to read, then core.setOutput('status', val) to output
process.env.INPUT_REPO to read, then core.setFailed('status') to output
core.getBooleanInput('repo') to read, then core.notice('status=' + val) to output

explanationCorrect: core.getInput reads a declared input by name, and core.setOutput writes a named output that consuming workflows read via steps.<id>.outputs.status.
explanationIncorrect: core.exportVariable creates an environment variable for later steps, not a step output, so status would not appear under steps.<id>.outputs. process.env.INPUT_REPO works to read the raw environment variable but core.setFailed marks the action as failed and does not set an output. core.getBooleanInput expects a boolean input and would mishandle a repository name, and core.notice creates an annotation message, not a structured output.

stem: How does a composite action step execute a shell command?

options.text: With a uses: key pointing at an inline shell action reference
With a run: key and an explicit shell: key specifying the shell
With a cmd: key that auto-detects the appropriate shell to use
With an exec: key that runs the command directly on the host runner

explanationCorrect: Inside a composite action, a step that runs commands must specify both run and an explicit shell, since composite steps require the shell to be named.
explanationIncorrect: A uses: key references another action, not an inline shell command. There is no cmd: key in composite action steps; auto-detection of shells is a workflow feature, not available in composite actions. There is no exec: key in the action step schema; the correct keys for running commands are run and shell.

stem: Which field in action.yml marks an input as required so the caller must provide it?

options.text: inputs.<name>.mandatory set to yes in the input declaration
inputs.<name>.default set to the string 'required' as a sentinel
runs.required listing the input names that must be supplied
inputs.<name>.required set to true in the input declaration

explanationCorrect: In action metadata, setting inputs.<name>.required to true tells consumers the input must be provided. Note that for composite and Docker actions, GitHub logs a warning but does not always hard-fail if required inputs are omitted.
explanationIncorrect: There is no mandatory field in the input schema; the field is called required. Setting default to the string 'required' just supplies a literal default value and does not enforce provision. runs.required is not a valid metadata field; input requirements are declared on each input individually.

stem: You release v2 of a popular action with breaking changes. How do you let existing users stay on v1 while new users adopt v2?

options.text: Delete the v1 tag and force all users to migrate immediately to v2
Keep a moving v1 major tag on the 1.x line and introduce a separate v2 tag
Rename the repository to signal the new version and create a fresh repo
Publish v2 only to the Marketplace while keeping v1 as a private action

explanationCorrect: Maintaining separate moving major tags (v1 and v2) lets existing users pin to @v1 for stability while new users opt into @v2's changes, following semantic versioning conventions.
explanationIncorrect: Deleting the v1 tag breaks every workflow pinned to it and is hostile to users. Renaming the repository changes all consumers' uses: paths and is disruptive rather than providing a migration path.
