Actions are public or private based on repository visibility, not per-version; you cannot have a public v2 and private v1 in the same repository.

stem: What is required to publish an action to the GitHub Marketplace so others can discover it?

options.text: Submit the action.yml to a central Marketplace registry via the GitHub CLI
A public repository with a valid action.yml and a published release
A private repository with a marketplace.json configuration file
Approval from GitHub's Marketplace review team before any listing appears

explanationCorrect: Actions gain discoverability by being published to the GitHub Marketplace from a public repository that contains a valid action metadata file and a tagged release.
explanationIncorrect: There is no central registry submission via the GitHub CLI; publishing happens through the repository's release workflow. A private repository cannot list an action on the public Marketplace. There is no marketplace.json configuration file. Actions do not require approval from a review team before listing; they are published through the release flow.

stem: A JavaScript action ships with a dist/ folder but no node_modules. A user reports that the action fails because a dependency is missing. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The bundler excluded a dependency that uses native bindings or dynamic require
The runner automatically runs npm install but the lockfile is outdated
The action.yml is missing a dependencies: field listing required packages
The Marketplace strips node_modules during the publishing process

explanationCorrect: Bundlers like ncc may fail to include dependencies that use native bindings, dynamic require(), or unusual module resolution, causing runtime failures when the bundled file misses them.
explanationIncorrect: The runner does not run npm install for actions; it executes the entry file directly, so lockfile state is irrelevant. There is no dependencies: field in action.yml; dependency management is the author's responsibility through bundling. The Marketplace does not strip node_modules; it serves whatever is committed to the repository at the tagged ref.

stem: Which section of action.yml documents the named values an action produces for downstream steps to consume?

options.text: The on: section, which defines triggers and their output payloads
The strategy: section, which maps matrix values to output names
The runs: section, which implicitly exports all set variables as outputs
The outputs: section, which declares each named value with a description

explanationCorrect: The outputs section of action.yml declares the named values the action produces so calling workflows can reference them via steps.<id>.outputs.<name>.
explanationIncorrect: The on: section defines workflow triggers and is not part of action metadata at all. The strategy: section configures matrices in workflows and is not part of action metadata. The runs: section defines how the action executes but does not implicitly export variables as outputs; outputs must be explicitly declared in the outputs: section.

stem: A composite action requires a specific CLI tool on the runner. What is a clean way to fail fast with a clear error if the tool is missing?

options.text: List the tool in a dependencies: field in action.yml so the runner installs it
Set continue-on-error: true on every step so failures are captured gracefully
Add an early composite step that checks for the tool and exits non-zero if absent
Add runs.pre: 'check-deps.sh' to run a pre-check script before main steps

explanationCorrect: An early composite step that verifies the tool (e.g., which <tool> || exit 1) and exits with a non-zero status when it is missing halts the action before the main logic runs, giving a clear failure message.
explanationIncorrect: There is no dependencies: field in action.yml; the action metadata does not manage tool installation. Setting continue-on-error: true would hide the very failure you want to surface, allowing subsequent steps to run and fail confusingly. runs.pre is a JavaScript action feature for running a script before main; composite actions have no pre: hook and must use their step sequence instead.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: ML training jobs require a specific NVIDIA GPU not available on any GitHub-hosted runner. How should the team run these jobs in GitHub Actions?

options.text: Use GitHub-hosted larger runners and request GPU acceleration in the workflow YAML
Register self-hosted runners on machines equipped with the required GPU hardware
Add a matrix entry for the GPU model so GitHub provisions a matching hosted runner
Set a service container with an nvidia/cuda image to emulate the GPU on a hosted runner

explanationCorrect: Self-hosted runners let you use your own hardware. Registering runners on GPU-equipped machines and labelling them appropriately lets workflows target the specific GPU resources GitHub-hosted runners do not offer.
explanationIncorrect: GitHub-hosted larger runners provide more CPU and memory but do not offer configurable GPU acceleration through workflow YAML. A matrix entry fans out job combinations but does not provision specialized hardware; GitHub selects runners by label, not by hardware request. A service container runs alongside the job for networked services but does not emulate GPU hardware; CUDA operations would fail without a physical GPU and appropriate drivers on the host.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An organization has two runner groups: build (open to all repos) and deploy-prod (restricted to three repos). A workflow in a non-authorized repository sets runs-on: [self-hosted, deploy-prod]. What is the outcome?

options.text: The job falls back to the build group because deploy-prod is unavailable
The job runs on a GitHub-hosted runner since no self-hosted runner matches
The job fails with an error indicating no runner matches the requested labels
The job queues indefinitely until a deploy-prod runner becomes available to that repository

explanationCorrect: When a repository is not in the runner group's access list, the runners in that group are invisible to it. Since no accessible runner carries the deploy-prod label, the job fails with a no-matching-runner error.
explanationIncorrect: Runner resolution does not fall back to other groups; if the requested label combination cannot be matched among accessible runners, the job fails. GitHub does not silently substitute a hosted runner when a self-hosted label is specified. The job does not queue indefinitely; GitHub determines runner availability at scheduling time and fails the job if no match exists.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: A workflow currently uses secrets.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and secrets.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY stored as repository secrets. What does adopting OIDC federation change about the workflow's secrets configuration?

options.text: The secrets must be moved to environment-level secrets and scoped to a deployment environment for OIDC to function
The AWS key secrets are removed and replaced by permissions: id-token: write plus an IAM role ARN
The secrets remain but are automatically rotated by GitHub's OIDC provider every 24 hours
The secrets are encrypted with the OIDC token before being passed to the AWS SDK

explanationCorrect: With OIDC federation, the workflow declares permissions: id-token: write and provides an IAM role ARN to the aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials action. The OIDC token is exchanged for temporary credentials at runtime, so the stored AWS key secrets can be deleted entirely.
explanationIncorrect: Moving secrets to environment level does not change their nature as long-lived credentials; OIDC's benefit is eliminating them, not relocating them. GitHub's OIDC provider issues per-run tokens for federation; it does not auto-rotate stored secrets. OIDC does not encrypt existing secrets; it replaces the need for them by providing a federated identity mechanism.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An ARC-managed runner scale set on Kubernetes has minRunners: 0 and maxRunners: 20. No jobs are queued. How many runner pods are currently running?

options.text: 20, because ARC always keeps the maximum number of pods warm and ready
1, because ARC maintains at least one idle pod regardless of the minimum setting
10, because ARC defaults to half of maxRunners when no jobs are queued
0, because minRunners: 0 allows the scale set to scale to zero when idle

explanationCorrect: When minRunners is set to 0 and no jobs are queued, ARC scales the runner scale set down to zero pods. Pods are only created when new jobs arrive in the queue.
explanationIncorrect: ARC does not keep maxRunners pods warm; it scales based on demand between the configured minimum and maximum. There is no built-in behavior to maintain one idle pod when the minimum is explicitly set to zero. ARC does not default to half of maxRunners; the scaling logic responds to the actual job queue depth within the min/max bounds.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An organization configures a required workflow via a ruleset. The required workflow references a reusable workflow in a private repository. Who needs access to that private repository for the required workflow to run in other repositories?

options.text: Every developer who opens a pull request in a targeted repository
Only the organization admin who configured the ruleset needs personal read access to the private repo
No one; required workflows have automatic access to any repository in the organization
The private repo must share its Actions access with the organization so the workflow can be fetched

explanationCorrect: For a required workflow that references a reusable workflow in a private repository, that private repository must have its Actions access settings configured to share with the organization. Without this, targeted repositories cannot fetch and execute the workflow.
explanationIncorrect: Individual developers do not need personal access to the private repository; the access is at the repository-to-repository level via Actions access settings. The admin who configured the ruleset does not grant runtime access through their own permissions. Required workflows do not have blanket automatic access to all repositories; the source repository must explicitly allow sharing.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: A self-hosted runner frequently runs jobs that hang indefinitely, consuming the machine for hours. Which setting prevents this without changing the workflow files?

options.text: Set a default timeout at the organization level in Actions settings
Add timeout-minutes to each job in every workflow file that uses the runner
Configure a concurrency group on the runner group to cancel stale runs
Set the runner's OS-level process timeout to kill any process after a fixed duration

explanationCorrect: Organization-level Actions settings can set a maximum job execution time that applies to workflows across repositories without modifying individual workflow files.
explanationIncorrect: Adding timeout-minutes to each workflow file works but requires editing every workflow, which the question explicitly rules out. Concurrency groups control run overlap, not individual job duration; a hanging job is not overlapping with another. An OS-level process timeout could kill the runner process itself, not just the job, potentially leaving the runner in a broken state and not properly reporting the failure back to GitHub.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: A repository's Actions tab shows 'Actions is not enabled for this repository.' The repository is public and belongs to an organization. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Public repositories never have access to GitHub Actions
The repository's branch protection rules are blocking all workflow triggers
The repository is missing a .github/workflows directory so Actions cannot initialize
The organization's Actions settings disable Actions for this repository or for all repositories

explanationCorrect: Organization Actions settings can disable Actions for all repositories, selected repositories, or specific ones. If this repository is excluded, the Actions tab shows it is not enabled.
explanationIncorrect: Public repositories have full access to GitHub Actions with generous included minutes. A missing .github/workflows directory means no workflows run, but the Actions tab still appears with options to set up workflows; it does not show 'not enabled.' Branch protection rules govern merging and do not disable Actions at the repository level.

stem: A non-critical linting step sometimes fails, but you want the job to continue to later steps regardless. Which key on that step allows this?

options.text: if: always() on the linting step to force it to run
continue-on-error: true on the linting step
strategy.fail-fast: false on the job to tolerate step failures
timeout-minutes: 0 on the linting step to skip it on failure

explanationCorrect: Setting continue-on-error: true on a step lets the job proceed to later steps even when that step returns a non-zero exit code. The step is marked as failed but the job continues.
explanationIncorrect: if: always() controls whether a step runs based on prior results — it does not affect how the step's own failure is handled, so later steps would still be skipped if the linting step fails. fail-fast controls matrix leg cancellation, not step-to-step flow within a single job. timeout-minutes: 0 is not valid for skipping failures — it sets a time limit, and zero would cause the step to be cancelled immediately. The correct key is continue-on-error.

stem: A workflow-level env var IMAGE_TAG is set to latest, but one job needs it set to canary. How do you override it for just that job?

options.text: Use $GITHUB_ENV in a step of that job to delete the workflow-level value
Redeclare it in the on: block with a per-job scope qualifier
Define IMAGE_TAG: canary in the env: block under that specific job
Set matrix.IMAGE_TAG: canary to override the workflow env for that job

explanationCorrect: A job-level env block sets variables scoped to that job and takes precedence over a workflow-level variable of the same name, so defining IMAGE_TAG: canary there overrides the workflow default for that job only.
explanationIncorrect: Writing to $GITHUB_ENV in a step appends new variables for subsequent steps but does not delete or retroactively override a workflow-level env value that was already injected — and the variable would already be set to 'latest' before that step runs. The on: block defines triggers and has no per-job scope qualifier for environment variables. Matrix values control job parallelization axes and do not override workflow-level env — they live in a separate context (matrix.<key>). The correct approach is a job-level env: block.

stem: When a caller invokes a reusable workflow, which runs-on value determines the runner for the called workflow's jobs?

options.text: The reusable workflow's own runs-on settings inside its job definitions
The caller's job-level runs-on, inherited by all called jobs automatically
A special runs-on: reusable label reserved for called workflow jobs
The organization's default runner group, overriding all runs-on values

explanationCorrect: A reusable workflow's jobs run on the runners specified by that workflow's own runs-on settings, independent of whatever runner the calling job uses.
explanationIncorrect: The caller's runs-on is not inherited by the called workflow; each workflow controls its own runner selection. There is no special reusable label for runners. The organization's default runner group does not override explicit runs-on values in workflow files.

stem: Your workflow references a popular action at owner/action@v3. A colleague reports that the maintainer's account was compromised and the v3 tag was repointed. What should you have done to prevent exposure?

options.text: Added permissions: {} to the job so the action could not access any GitHub APIs
Used a fork of the action in your own organization instead of the upstream
Pinned uses to the full commit SHA of the reviewed v3 release instead of the tag
Set continue-on-error: true so a compromised step would not fail the pipeline

explanationCorrect: Pinning to the full commit SHA of the reviewed release makes the reference immutable; even if the v3 tag is repointed by a compromised account, the workflow still runs the original safe code.
explanationIncorrect: Dropping all permissions limits API access but does not prevent the compromised code from executing, exfiltrating data, or injecting into outputs. Forking shifts maintenance burden and can still drift if not kept up to date, and does not inherently prevent tag manipulation in the fork. continue-on-error only changes whether a failure blocks the run; it does not prevent compromised code from executing and causing damage.

stem: A custom action lives at .github/actions/lint in the same repository as the workflow. After actions/checkout runs, which uses reference calls it?

options.text: uses: actions/lint@main referencing the action by short name and branch
uses: .github/actions/lint without the leading ./ prefix
run: .github/actions/lint/action.yml executed as a shell script
uses: ./.github/actions/lint as a relative path to the action directory

explanationCorrect: A local action in the same repository is referenced by a relative path starting with ./ that points to the directory containing its action.yml, so ./.github/actions/lint is correct.
explanationIncorrect: actions/lint@main is the format for a remote action in another repository, not a local path reference. Omitting the leading ./ makes it an ambiguous path that GitHub does not resolve as a local action. action.yml is a metadata file, not a shell script, so running it with run: would fail.

stem: Why must each run step in a composite action specify a shell, unlike workflow run steps that infer one?

options.text: Composite actions always run on a different OS than the calling workflow
Composite actions have no defaults.run.shell equivalent, so each step must be explicit
The shell key actually selects the runner image, not the command interpreter
It is a deprecated requirement that GitHub plans to remove in a future release

explanationCorrect: Unlike workflows, which can infer the shell from the runner OS or set defaults.run.shell, composite actions have no default shell mechanism. Each run step must explicitly name its shell.
explanationIncorrect: Composite actions run on the same runner as the calling workflow, not a different OS. The shell key selects the command interpreter (bash, pwsh, etc.), not the runner image; runs-on controls the runner. This requirement is a design choice, not a deprecated behavior; GitHub has not announced plans to add default shell inference for composite actions.

stem: Which runs.using value in action.yml declares a JavaScript action?

options.text: docker, which runs JavaScript inside a Node container automatically
composite, which compiles JavaScript steps into a single action
javascript, the dedicated runtime value for JS-based actions
node20, specifying the Node.js runtime version directly

explanationCorrect: A JavaScript action sets runs.using to a Node runtime version such as node20 and points main at its compiled entry file.
explanationIncorrect: docker indicates a container action that runs an image, not JavaScript directly; it does not auto-detect or run Node. composite indicates an action composed of multiple steps and does not imply JavaScript execution. There is no 'javascript' value for runs.using; the valid values are node-version strings (node20), docker, and composite.

stem: Which field in action.yml gives an input a documented default value that applies when the caller does not supply it?

options.text: inputs.<name>.value, which sets the initial and default value together
outputs.<name>.default, which feeds back into the input automatically
inputs.<name>.default, which supplies the fallback value
runs.defaults.<name>, which sets all input defaults in one block

explanationCorrect: The default field on an input supplies the value used when the caller does not provide that input, and it is documented in the action's metadata for consumers to see.
explanationIncorrect: There is no value field on an input; the field for fallback values is called default. The outputs section describes values the action produces, not input defaults, and there is no feedback mechanism between them. There is no runs.defaults block for input defaults; each input declares its own default individually.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An organization creates a variable named DEPLOY_REGION at the organization level. A repository also defines a variable with the same name. Which value does a workflow in that repository read from vars.DEPLOY_REGION?

options.text: The organization-level value, because organization scope always takes precedence
The workflow fails because duplicate variable names across levels are not allowed
The repository-level value, because the more specific scope overrides the broader one
Both values concatenated, separated by a comma

explanationCorrect: Configuration variables follow the same precedence rules as secrets: the most specific level wins. A repository-level variable overrides an organization-level variable with the same name.
explanationIncorrect: Organization scope is the broadest and is overridden by more specific levels, not the other way around. Duplicate names across levels are expected and resolved by precedence; they do not cause failures. Values are never concatenated; a single value is selected based on the override chain.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An environment named staging has a 15-minute wait timer and two required reviewers. A deploy job targets this environment. In what order do the protections apply?

options.text: The wait timer and reviewer approval run in parallel; whichever finishes last unblocks the job
The reviewer approval must complete first, then the wait timer starts
The wait timer runs first, then the reviewer approval is requested
Only the stricter protection applies; the other is ignored

explanationCorrect: When multiple environment protection rules are configured, they evaluate concurrently. The wait timer begins counting and the reviewer approval request goes out at the same time. The job is unblocked only when all protection rules are satisfied, so whichever completes last determines when the job starts.
explanationIncorrect: The protections are not sequential in either order; GitHub evaluates all environment protection rules concurrently rather than chaining them. The wait timer begins counting down at the same time the reviewer approval request is sent, so if reviewers approve before the timer expires the job waits only for the remaining timer duration. GitHub does not select only the stricter protection and ignore the other; every configured rule must be independently satisfied before the job is allowed to proceed.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: A persistent self-hosted runner handles jobs from multiple repositories. After a job from an untrusted fork, the next job from a different repository finds unexpected environment variables set. What runner configuration prevents cross-job state leakage?

options.text: Adding the runner to a concurrency group so only one job runs across all repositories
Configuring the runner as ephemeral with the --ephemeral flag during registration
Setting permissions: {} on every workflow to strip the GITHUB_TOKEN of all scopes
Moving the runner to a runner group with a wait timer protection rule

explanationCorrect: Registering a runner with --ephemeral makes it handle exactly one job and then de-register itself. The runner process exits after the job completes, and a new clean instance must be started for the next job, eliminating cross-job state leakage.
explanationIncorrect: A concurrency group serializes overlapping workflow runs but does not clean the runner between sequential jobs; environment variables and files still persist on a non-ephemeral runner. Stripping the GITHUB_TOKEN of scopes limits API access within a job but does not prevent a job from setting environment variables or writing files that the next job inherits. Wait timer protection rules are an environment feature that delays job start; they do not clean the runner between jobs.
